parole.significato: With stronger or greater reason; as a corollary implied by a stronger claim; even more so; all the more so; so much the…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Medieval Latin ā fortiōrī.

parole.significato: Involving induction of theories from facts.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ā posteriōrī (“involving reasoning from effect to cause, from experience to theory”, literally “from what follows”). Popularized from the 19th century in reference to the work of Immanuel Kant.

parole.significato: Self-evident, intuitively obvious.
parole.testo: First attested in 1610. Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ā priōrī (“involving reasoning from cause to effect; from first principles”, literally “from the former”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Levite.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Aaronida under influence from French aaronide, from Koine Greek Αἀρωνίδης (Aarōnídēs) in the Septuagint. Equivalent to Aaron + -id.

parole.significato: One who uses an abacus in casting accounts; a calculator.
parole.testo: From Middle English abaciste, from Medieval Latin abacista, from abacus + -ista (“-ist”).

parole.significato: A retaining wall; a wall erected to strengthen another wall.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin abamūrus.

parole.significato: A member of the dynasty of caliphs that ruled from Baghdad, from about 750 to 1250, claiming ancestry of Abbas.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Abbasidēs, from Abbas + -idēs (patronymic suffix). By surface analysis, Abbas + -id (dynastic suffix).

parole.significato: An abridgment; a compendium; an abstract.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin abbreviātūra, from Late Latin abbreviō (“shorten, abbreviate”). See also abbreviate.

parole.significato: A concealed location used for storage or to hide items.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin abditorium, from abdō (“to hide”).

parole.significato: A muscle which serves to draw a part out, or from the median line of the body
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin abductor, from abdūcō + -tor.

parole.significato: The alphabet, written out in a teaching book, or carved on a wall; a primer; abecedarium.
parole.testo: From Middle English abscedary, from Medieval Latin abecedārium (“alphabet, ABC primer”), from Late Latin abecedārius (“of the alphabet”), formed from the first four letters of the Latin alphabet + -ārius. Doublet of abecedarium.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Aberdeen.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Aberdonia (“Aberdeen”) + -an.

parole.significato: Producing abrasion; rough enough to wear away the outer surface.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin abrāsīvus.

parole.significato: To renounce; to contradict.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin abrenunciare, from Latin ab- (“from”) + renuntio (“revoke”).

parole.significato: A bushy wormwood from Europe, sometimes used in the brewing of beer, southernwood, Artemisia abrotanum.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin, from Latin abrotonum, from Ancient Greek ἀβρότονον (abrótonon, “wormwood, southernwood”).

parole.significato: A colorless crystalline alkaloid obtained from abrotanum, C₂₁H₂₂N₂O.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin abrotanum (“wormwood”) + -ine.

parole.significato: The act of absenting oneself.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin absentatio, from Latin absento (“to be absent”). Equivalent to absent + -ation.

parole.significato: Having an abstracting nature or tendency; tending to separate; tending to be withdrawn.
parole.testo: From Middle English abstractif, from Medieval Latin abstractivus, from Latin abstractus (“drawn away”) + -ivus (“-ive”). Equivalent to abstract + -ive.

parole.significato: A title used in medieval Scotland.
parole.testo: There are two etymologies suggested for this word, each peculiar to a different suggested meaning. parole.significato: To touch by means of a mutual border, edge or end; to border on; to lie adjacent (to); to be contiguous (said of an are…
parole.testo: From Middle English abutten, from Medieval Latin abuttare and Old French abuter, aboter, abouter (“to touch at one end, to come to an end, aim, reach”), from Old French but (“end, aim, purpose”); akin to Old Norse butr (“piece of wood”). Equivalent to a- (“to”) + butt (“boundary mark”).

parole.significato: Belonging to, or resembling, an abyss; unfathomable.
parole.testo: First attested in the 1690s. From Medieval Latin abyssalis, from Latin abyssus (“abyss”) + -alis (“-al”). Equivalent to abyss + -al.

parole.significato: To pronounce with an accent or vocal stress.
parole.testo: First attested in 1731; borrowed from Medieval Latin accentuātus, perfect passive participle of accentuō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin accentus. accent + -u- + -ate.

parole.significato: Someone who accedes to some act, now especially a crime; one who contributes as an assistant or instigator to the commi…
parole.testo: From Middle English accessarie, axcessary, excercary, from Medieval Latin accessārius.

parole.significato: Accompanying as a subordinate; additional; accessory; especially, uniting in, or contributing to, a crime, but not as c…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin accessārius.

parole.significato: Having a secondary, supplementary or subordinate function by accompanying as a subordinate; aiding in a secondary way;…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin accessōrius, from Latin accessor (“helper, subordinate”), from accessus. Compare access, from same root.

parole.significato: To summon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin accitō (“summon”), from Classical Latin acciō (“call forth”), formed from ad + cieō (“summon, call”). The sense “excite, induce” is likely from or reinforced by conflation with excite.

parole.significato: Tending to accomplish.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin accompletivus.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the sense of hearing, the organs of hearing, or the science of sounds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin acousticus, acūsticus, from Ancient Greek ἀκουστῐκός (akoustĭkós, “of or for hearing”), from ἀκούω (akoúō, “to hear”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: To activate, or to put into motion; to animate.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin āctuātus, perfect passive participle of āctuō (“actuate, implement”), from Latin āctus, perfect passive participle of agō (“do, act”).

parole.significato: Sharpened; sharp-pointed.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin acuātus, past participle of acuāre, variant of Classical Latin acuere (“to sharpen”), from acus (“needle”).

parole.significato: Synonym of acuation (“act of sharpening”).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin acuitio (“whetting, sharpening”), from acuo (“sharpen”). By surface analysis, acuity + -ion.

parole.significato: Capable of being added; thus:
parole.testo: From add + -ible, perhaps after Medieval Latin addibilis.

parole.significato: equivalent or sufficient; adequate.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin adaequātivus, from Latin adaequō (“make equal to”).

parole.significato: The state or quality of being adherent; adherence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin adhaerentia.

parole.significato: A room in a temple for the adoration of idols.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin adōrātōrium.

parole.significato: An external addition.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin advention (“addition”), ultimately from Latin adveniō (“to arrive”).

parole.significato: From an external source; not innate or inherent, foreign.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin adventītius (“coming from abroad, extraneous”), a corruption of Latin adventīcius (“foreign, strange, accidental”), from adventus (“arrival, coming, approach, advent”) + -īcius (suffix forming adjectives), from adveniō (“to arrive”) + -tus (suffix forming action nouns).

parole.significato: Synonym of verdigrisy, of or related to copper carbonate, bluish green.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin aerūginōsus (“rust-colored”) directly and via Middle French erugineux (“verdigris-colored”), from Latin aerūginōsus (“rusty”), from aerūgō (“rust”) + -ōsus (“-ose: forming adjectives”), from aes (“copper, bronze, brass”) + -ūgō (“forming nouns related to thin coatings or covering

parole.significato: Relating to, resulting from, or influenced by the emotions.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin affectivus, from Latin affectus, past participle of afficere (“to affect”). By surface analysis, affect + -ive.

parole.significato: A signed document wherein an affiant makes a sworn statement.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin affidavit (“he has sworn”), the third person singular perfect tense of affido (“swear”), from fīdō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ- (“to command, to persuade, to trust”). parole.significato: Someone or something, especially, a television station, that is associated with a larger, related organization, such as…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin affīliātus, the passive past participle of Late Latin adfīliō, affīliō (“to adopt as son”), from ad- + fīlius + -ō. Equivalent to Latin affīliō + -ate. Compare French affilié (noun).

parole.significato: To make into forest
parole.testo: First attested in the 16th century. From Medieval Latin afforēstō, from Latin ad (“towards”) + forēsta (“forest”).

parole.significato: The act or process of creating a new forest where none had existed before, or reforestation of areas long deforested.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin afforestātiō, from afforestāt-, past participial stem of afforestō (“to convert into a forest”) (from Latin ad- + Late Latin forestis (“forest”) + -ō (suffix forming verbs)), + Latin -iō (suffix forming action nouns). By surface analysis, afforest + -ation.

parole.significato: The capacity, condition, or state of acting or of exerting power.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin agentia, from Latin agēns (present participle of agere (“to act”)), agentis (cognate with French agence, see also agent).

parole.significato: The act of producing in addition.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin aggeneratio (“generating in addition”), from aggenerat- (past participle stem of aggenerare) + io (“-ion”).

parole.significato: The inhabitants of Albi, a city in southern France.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin, from French Albi.

parole.significato: Any of a class of organic compounds (such as ethanol) containing a hydroxyl functional group (-OH).
parole.testo: First attested in the 15th century from Middle English alcofol, from Middle French alcohol or Spanish alcohol, derived from the Medieval Latin rendering alcohol transmitted in medical or alchemical literature of Arabic اَلْكُحْل (al-kuḥl, “kohl”), which in Andalusian Arabic also bore the form كُحُول

parole.significato: A cauldron of boiling water into which an accused person plunged his forearm, used as a form of trial in Medieval Engla…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin alfetum, from Old English alfæt (“fire-vat”), from āl (“fire”) + fæt (“vat”).

parole.significato: Elementary algebra: A system for representing and manipulating unknown quantities (variables) in equations.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin algebra, from the Arabic الْجَبْر (al-jabr, “reunion, resetting of broken parts”) in the title of al-Khwarizmi's influential work الْكِتَاب الْمُخْتَصَر فِي حِسَاب الْجَبْر وَالْمُقَابَلَة (al-kitāb al-muḵtaṣar fī ḥisāb al-jabr wa-l-muqābala, “The Compendious Book on Cal

parole.significato: The state of being different; otherness.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin alietas, from Latin alius (“other”). By surface analysis, Latin ali(us) + -e- + -ty.

parole.significato: An allurement, enticement.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin allectīvus (“that allures”).

parole.significato: Freehold land or property; land held in allodial tenure, or one's title to such land.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin allodium, from Frankish *allaaud (“allodium, patrimony”, literally “entire property”), from Frankish *all (“all”) + *aud (“owndom, possessions”). Cognate with Old High German ōt (“property”), Old Saxon ōd (“estate, wealth”), Old English ēad (“possessions”).

parole.significato: Any of the different realisations of a termineme under a specific domain or environment. For instance, [MORPHOLOGY]_(TE…
parole.testo: Analogous to allophone, allomorph, from allo- + Medieval Latin terminus (“a term”).

parole.significato: soil, clay, silt or gravel deposited by flowing water, as it slows, in a river bed, delta, estuary or flood plain
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin alluvium (“matter deposited by flowing water”), neuter of alluvius (“deposited by a river”), from Latin alluviō (“washing upon, overflowing”). See also al-.

parole.significato: Pompous, or pretentious in speech
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin altiloquus, from altus (“high, tall”) and -loquus (“speaking”).

parole.significato: A pear-shaped pot with an opening at each end, formerly used, especially by alchemists, for sublimation.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin aludel, from Arabic الأُثَال (al-ʔuṯāl, “the sublimation vessel”).

parole.significato: An alloy containing mercury.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin amalgama (“mercury alloy”), from Arabic اَلْمَلْغَم (al-malḡam, “emollient poultice or unguent for sores”), from Ancient Greek μάλαγμα (málagma, “emollient; malleable material”), from μαλάσσω (malássō, “to soften”), from μαλακός (malakós, “soft”). parole.significato: To merge, to combine, to blend, to join.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin amalgamātus, past participle of amalgamāre, amalgama.

parole.significato: The process of amalgamating; a mixture, merger or consolidation.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin amalgamātiō.

parole.significato: Pertaining to love; amorous.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin amātīvus, from Latin amātus, perfect passive participle of amō (“love”).

parole.significato: Someone who is ambidextrous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ambidexter, from Latin ambi- + dexter.

parole.significato: The property of being equally skillful with each hand.
parole.testo: Dating from the 17th century C.E.; ambidexter + -ity, from Medieval Latin adjective ambidexter (“utilising both hands normally”), from Latin ambi- + dexter (“right, handy, opportune”).

parole.significato: Using ambiguous expressions; speaking or writing in a way that may be variously interpreted.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ambiloquus, from Classical Latin ambi- (“both”) + -loquus (“speaking”). By surface analysis, ambiloquy + -ous.

parole.significato: Ambiguous language.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ambiloquium, from ambiloquus + Classical Latin -ium, from Classical Latin ambi- (“both”) + -loquus (“speaking”). By surface analysis, ambi- + -loquy.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being amicable or friendly.
parole.testo: From amicable + -ability, perhaps after Medieval Latin amīcābilitās. Piecewise doublet of amiability.

parole.significato: Of or relating to ammonia, or possessing its properties.
parole.testo: From Middle English ammoniak, from Medieval Latin ammōniacum.

parole.significato: Each one of the two regions of the brain, located as a pair in the medial temporal lobe, believed to play a key role in…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin amygdala (“almond, amygdala”), from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē, “almond”), named as such due to its shape. Doublet of almond, amygdale, and mandorla.

parole.significato: Decomposition into components in order to study (a complex thing, concept, theory, etc.).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin analysis, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλυσις (análusis), from ἀναλύω (analúō, “to unravel, investigate”), from ἀνα- (ana-, “thoroughly”) + λύω (lúō, “to loosen”).

parole.significato: Lacking echoes; particularly, designed to absorb sound.
parole.testo: From an- + echoic, from echo + -ic, from Middle English ecco, ekko, from Medieval Latin ecco, from Latin echo, from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ), from ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound”).

parole.significato: Relating to the Church of England, or one of several related churches, such as those in the Anglican Communion.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin Anglicānus, from anglicus (“English, Englishman”) + -ānus (“-an: forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: Addition or incorporation of something, or territories that have been annexed.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin annexation-, stem of annexatio (“action of annexing”), from past participle of annecto.

parole.significato: A day that is an exact number of years (to the day) since a given significant event occurred. Often preceded by an ordi…
parole.testo: From Middle English anniversary, from Medieval Latin anniversāria (diēs), anniversārium, from anniversārius (“yearly”), from annus (“year”) + versus, past participle of vertere (“to turn”).

parole.significato: In the year of our Lord (often abbreviated A.D. or AD).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin annō Dominī (“in the year of the Lord”) from the word annō (“in the year”) the ablative of annus (“year”) + Dominī (“of the Lord”) the genitive of Dominus (“the Lord”).

parole.significato: The current date era beginning approximately 2000 years ago in the Gregorian calendar, based on the birth of Jesus Chri…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin annō Dominī, from annō, (ablative of annus (“year”)) + Dominī (genitive of dominus (“lord”)); literally, in the year of the Lord.

parole.significato: A ring- or donut-shaped area, object, or structure.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ānnulus, a misspelling of Latin ānulus (“ring, especially one worn on a finger”), from ānus (“ring”) (possibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eh₂-n-o- (“ring”), from an uncertain root) + -ulus (diminutive suffix). parole.significato: To announce.
parole.testo: From annunciātus, Medieval Latin alternative spelling of annuntiātus, past participle of Latin annūntiāre. Doublet of announce.

parole.significato: Capable of soothing or eliminating pain.
parole.testo: From Middle English anodine, from Medieval Latin anōdynos (“stilling or relieving pain”), from Ancient Greek ἀνώδυνος (anṓdunos, “free from pain”), from ἀν- (an-, “without”) + ὀδύνη (odúnē, “pain”). parole.significato: Before noon, in the morning.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Medieval Latin ante merīdiem, from Latin ante (“before”) + merīdiem, accusative singular of merīdiēs (“noon, midday”).

parole.testo: From Medieval Latin antimonium, attested in the 11th century; see also the Wikipedia section.

parole.significato: One who embraces, encourages, or practices antinomianism.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Antinomi, from Ancient Greek ἀντί (antí, “against”) + νόμος (nómos, “custom, law”).

parole.significato: Tending to open the bowels; aperient.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin aperitivus, from Late Latin apertivus, from Latin aperio. Doublet of apéritif, from French.

parole.significato: To be grateful or thankful for.
parole.testo: Originated 1645–55; from Medieval Latin appreciātus (“valued or appraised”), later variant of Late Latin appretiātus (“appraised”), the perfect passive participle of appretiō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from a(d) (“toward”) + preti(um) (“price”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix). parole.significato: Expressing approval.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin approbātīvus, from Latin approbō (“assert, accept, confirm”).

parole.significato: An act or instance of appropriating.
parole.testo: From Middle English appropriacion, appropriacioun, from Medieval Latin appropriātiō. By surface analysis, appropriate + -ion.

parole.significato: An aqueous solution of alcohol typically prepared by distilling wine.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin aqua vītae directly and via Middle English aqua vite and French eau-de-vie, from aqua (“water”) and vītae (“of life”). Doublet of aquavit and akvavit. Compare eau de vie, whisky, whiskey, and water of life from the same source.

parole.significato: A ewer or jug-like vessel, shaped like an animal or human figure, used for washing the hands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin aquamanile, from Latin aqua (“water”), and the root of manus (“hand”).

parole.significato: A number represented using an Indian and Arabic system involving the symbols 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 0, represen…
parole.testo: A calque of Medieval Latin numerus Arabicus, from its gradual adoption in Europe from Arabic sources.

parole.significato: A diocese administered by an archbishop.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Medieval Latin archdiocesis, variant of archidioecēsis, from archi- (“chief, main”) + Late Latin dioecēsis, q.v., equivalent to arch- + diocese.

parole.significato: Of or relating to argumentation; specifically, presenting a logical argument or line of reasoning; argumentive, discurs…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English argumentatif (“syllogistic, sophistic”), from Old French argumentatif, argumentative (modern French argumentatif (“argumentative”)) and Medieval Latin, Late Latin argūmentātīvus, from Latin argūmentātor + -īvus (suffix forming adjectives).

parole.significato: A resinous gum from the stem and roots of Ferula species such as Ferula foetida and Ferula assa-foetida, having a stron…
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Medieval Latin asafoetida, from Persian ازا / آزا (azâ, âzâ, “mastic”) + Latin foetida, feminine of foetidus (“bad-smelling”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to ascetics.
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1646. From Medieval Latin asceticus, from Ancient Greek ἀσκητικός (askētikós), from ἀσκητής (askētḗs, “monk, hermit”), from ἀσκέω (askéō, “to exercise”).

parole.significato: The attribute of being entirely self-derived, in contrast to being derived from or dependent on another; the quality of…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin aseitas (“state of being by itself”), from Classical Latin a se + -itas.

parole.significato: Any of various perennial plants of the genus Asparagus having leaflike stems, scalelike leaves, and small flowers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin asparagus, sparagus, from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos), variant of ἀσφάραγος (aspháragos). Displaced Old English eorþnafola. Later became an eggcorn in dialect as sparrowgrass.

parole.significato: Boldly self-assured; confident without being aggressive.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin assertīvus. Synchronically analyzable as assert + -ive.

parole.significato: The act of assimilating or the state of being assimilated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin assimilatio. By surface analysis, assimilate + -ion.

parole.significato: A long-term respiratory condition, in which the airways may unexpectedly and suddenly narrow, often in response to an a…
parole.testo: From Middle English asma, asme, from Medieval Latin asthma, asma, from Ancient Greek ἆσθμα (âsthma, “laborious breathing, asthma”). The spelling was changed to add -th- in the 16th century to match the Greek etymological roots.

parole.significato: A state of being found guilty of an offence.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin attinctūra, used to translate Old French ateint, from Vulgar Latin *attinctus (perfect passive participle of Latin attingō).

parole.significato: Insolent boldness, especially when imprudent or unconventional.
parole.testo: From Middle English audacite, from Medieval Latin audācitās (whence -acity), from Latin audāx (“bold”), from audeō (“to be bold, to dare”).

parole.significato: A condition of absolute power.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin autarchia, from Koine Greek αὐταρχία (autarkhía, “absolute power, sovereignty, autocracy”), from αὔταρχος (aútarkhos, “autocratic”), from αὐτ- (aut-, “self”) + ἄρχω (árkhō, “to rule, govern”).

parole.significato: To render authentic; to give authority to, by the proof, attestation, or formalities required by law, or sufficient to…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin authenticō. By surface analysis, authentic + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: In the manner of an uncle, pertaining to an uncle.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin avunculāris, from Classical Latin avunculus (“maternal uncle”) + -āris (“-ar”).

parole.significato: sura (chapter of the Qurʾān)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin azoara.

parole.significato: Synonym of bailey (“fortification”).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ballium.

parole.significato: An ethnic descendant of the Indo-European Baltic people, especially including ethnic Lithuanians, Latvians or Prussians…
parole.testo: Back-formation from Baltic and/or Medieval Latin and Late Latin Balthae; see Baltic for more.

parole.significato: A tree, Adansonia digitata, native to tropical Africa, having a broad swollen trunk and edible gourd-like hanging fruit…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bahobab, from Arabic أَبُو حِبَاب (ʔabū ḥibāb, “father of many seeds”), from أَبُو (ʔabū, “father”) + حَبّ (ḥabb, “seed”).

parole.significato: Relating to people, countries, or customs perceived as uncivilized or inferior.
parole.testo: From Middle English barbarian, borrowed from Medieval Latin barbarinus (“Berber, pagan, foreigner”), from Latin barbaria (“foreign country”), from barbarus (“foreigner, savage”), from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros, “foreign, non-Greek, strange”), possibly onomatopoeic (mimicking foreign languages

parole.significato: Any of the thorny shrubs of genus Berberis, which bear yellow flowers and red or blue-black berries.
parole.testo: From Middle English berberie, from Medieval Latin berberis (on which see Arabic بَرْبَارِيس (barbārīs)), influenced by berie (“berry”). Doublet of berberis and related to Berber.

parole.significato: A board fastened to the projecting gables of a roof to protect and hide other timbers.
parole.testo: Probably from Medieval Latin bargus (“a scaffold”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Gnostic sect founded by Basilides of Alexandria in the 2nd century.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Basilidiānus, from Byzantine Greek Βασιλειδιανός (Basileidianós). By surface analysis, Basilides + -ian.

parole.significato: An administrative official at universities in several European countries, often with a policiary function at the time w…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pedellus, bedellus, bidellus, from Middle English bedel; cognate with beadle.

parole.significato: Any of various plants imported into Europe for the pharmaceutical trade in dried form, so of uncertain identity.
parole.testo: A Medieval Latin transcription of the Arabic بَهْمَن (bahman).

parole.significato: Somebody who gives a gift, often money to a charity.
parole.testo: From Middle English benefactor, borrowed from Medieval Latin benefactor (“he who bestows a favor”), from Latin benefaciō (“benefit someone”), from bene (“good”) + faciō (“do, make”).

parole.significato: A medieval treatise of various real or imaginary animals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bēstiārium, from Latin bēstia (“beast, animal”). By surface analysis, beast + -ary.

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Stachys.
parole.testo: From Middle English betayny, betanie, from Medieval Latin betōnia (possibly through Old French), from Latin betōnica or ve(t)tōnica, from Vettones, a people in Lusitania. Compare French bétoine.

parole.significato: A specific version, edition, translation, or copy of one of the above-mentioned texts.
parole.testo: From Middle English bible, from Medieval Latin biblia (“book”) (misinterpreted as a feminine from earlier Latin neuter plural biblia (“books”)), from Ancient Greek βιβλία (biblía, “books”), plural of βιβλίον (biblíon, “small book”), originally a diminutive of βίβλος (bíblos, “book”), from βύβλος (bú

parole.significato: Biblical.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin biblicus, analyzable as bible + -ic.

parole.significato: To divide or fork into two channels or branches.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin bifurcātus. Surface Analysis bi- + furcate.

parole.significato: Divided into two branches.
parole.testo: From verb bifurcate, from Medieval Latin bifurcatus, past participle of bifurcare, from Latin bifurcus (“two-pronged”), from bi- + furca (“fork”).

parole.significato: to buzz or hum; to speak idly, vacuously, or to little effect.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin bombināre (“buzz, hum”), variant of Latin bombilō, from Ancient Greek βομβυλιάζειν (bombuliázein), from βόμβος (bómbos, “booming, humming”), of imitative origin.

parole.significato: The state of being enslaved or the practice of slavery.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English bondage (“serfdom”), from British Medieval Latin bondagium (“an inferior tenure held by a bond or husbandman”), from Middle English bond (“tenant farmer, serf”), from Old English bonda (“householder, husband, head of a family”), of Old Norse origin. parole.significato: Relating to, or impregnated with borax.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin borax (genitive boracis), itself via Arabic بَوْرَق (bawraq), from Persian بوره (bura).

parole.significato: Synonym of bordar (“person ranking below villeins and above serfs”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bordarius, from Old French borde (“hut, cabin, small farm”) + -arius.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to botany.
parole.testo: From the Medieval Latin botanicus, perhaps via the French botanique, from the Ancient Greek βοτανικός (botanikós), from βοτάνη (botánē, “herb, pasture”).

parole.significato: Synonym of oxgang.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin bovāta, from Latin bov-, bōs + -āta.

parole.significato: A coward.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Bretany, Brytany, itself borrowed from Medieval Latin Britannia, applied to Brittany from at least the 6th century, and reinforced by Middle French Bretagne. See Britannia for more. Doublet of Britain and Britannia.

parole.significato: Of a dark brown colour.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin brunneus (“brown”), derived from Proto-Germanic *brūnaz (“brown”).

parole.significato: Savagely violent, vicious, ruthless, or cruel, often in an unintelligent manner.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin brutalis (“savage, stupid”), from Latin brūtus (“dull, stupid”).

parole.significato: An inflamed swelling of a lymph node, especially in the armpit or groin, due to an infection such as bubonic plague, go…
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Medieval Latin būbō, from Ancient Greek βουβών (boubṓn, “groin, swelling”).

parole.significato: A member of a migratory Turkic people from Central Asia who conquered Moesia in the 7th century and settled what is now…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Bulgarus, from Old Church Slavonic блъгаринъ (blŭgarinŭ), itself from the self designation of Turkic Bulgars, from Proto-Turkic *bulgar (“disturber, disturbing”), active noun/adjective of *bulga- (“to create a state of disorder; to stir, to disturb”). parole.significato: Synonym of bullary (“a collection of papal bulls”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bullarium, from bulla (“seal; papal bull”) + -arium.

parole.significato: A person who breaks in to premises with the intent of committing a crime, usually theft.
parole.testo: 16th century, from Medieval Latin burglātor, British byform of burgātor (“burglar”), derived from burgō (“to commit burglary”), from Late Latin burgus (“fortified town”), itself probably from Frankish *burg (“fortress”), from Proto-Germanic *burgz, *burgiją (“borough, watch-tower”). parole.significato: Any of the many small fluid-filled sacs located at the point where a muscle or tendon slides across bone. These sacs se…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bursa (“purse”), from Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa); compare purse and bourse, which are doublets.

parole.significato: The treasurer of a university, college or school.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bursārius, from bursa (“purse”) (English purse).

parole.significato: A monetary award to university students that allows them to continue their studies.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bursaria, from bursarius.

parole.significato: A mythical bird that had healing powers.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin caladrius, from Byzantine Greek χαλαδριός (khaladriós), from Ancient Greek χαραδριός (kharadriós).

parole.significato: The room or building in a monastery holding its communal fire, kept warm and used as a sitting room.
parole.testo: * Borrowed from Medieval Latin calefactorium.

parole.significato: Monarchical government based on a claim of succession to the Islamic State of Muhammad, ruled by a caliph.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin calīphātus, equivalent to caliph + -ate.

parole.significato: A metal object, usually small, with spikes arranged so that, when thrown onto the ground, one always faces up as a thre…
parole.testo: From Middle English calketrappe, from Old English calcatrippe, from Medieval Latin calcatrippa (“thistle”), from Latin calx or calcare (“to tread”) + trappa (“trap”).

parole.significato: A chicken of a breed originating from the aforementioned region.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Campania

parole.significato: A type of canon in which the imitating voice repeats the notes of the theme in reverse order
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin, present participle of cancrizāre (“to go backwards”), from Latin cancr-, cancer (“crab”) + Late Latin -izāre (“-ize”).

parole.significato: Present in a canon, religious or otherwise.
parole.testo: From Middle English canonycal, from Medieval Latin canōnicālis. By surface analysis, canon + -ical.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a capitulum.
parole.testo: From Middle English capituler, from Medieval Latin capitulāris, from Latin capitulum (“a small head, a chapter”).

parole.significato: To surrender on stipulated terms, end all resistance, give up, go along with or comply.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in 1528, the verb in 1537; borrowed from Medieval Latin capitulātus perfect passive participle of Medieval Latin capitulō (“(originally; of a book, text) to draw up under distinct headings; (from the 15ᵗʰ c.) to bargain, parley, convene”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffi

parole.significato: A biennial plant of species Carum carvi, native to Europe and Asia, mainly grown for its seed to be used as a culinary…
parole.testo: From Middle English caraway, carewey, carwey, from Medieval Latin carui, from Arabic كَرَاوِيَا (karāwiyā), via Aramaic from Ancient Greek καρώ (karṓ), κάρον (káron, “caraway”).

parole.significato: A 40-day fast or period of similar abstinence.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin carēna (“40-day fast; remission of such a fast”), from Late Latin quadragēna (“40-day period, Lent”) or quarantena (“40-day period”), from Latin quadrāgēnus (“40 each”), from quadrāgintā (“four tens, forty”). Doublet of quadragene.

parole.significato: Carnelian.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin carneolus (“carnelian”), diminutive of Latin carneus (“fleshy”).

parole.significato: A descendant of Charles Martel; a Carolingian.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Carolingus, from a Frankish patronymic ultimately composed of Proto-West Germanic *karil + *-ing. By surface analysis, Carolus + -ing.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Carolings, the members of a Frankish dynasty, descended from Charles Martel, which arose from t…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Carolingī (“Carolings (descendants of Charles Martel)”) [plural of Carolingus, from a Frankish patronymic ultimately composed of Proto-West Germanic *karil + *-ing] + -ian. Reshaping of earlier Carlovingian, from Middle French Carlovingien, itself a misconstruction of Carlingien.

parole.significato: A heavy wheeled turnplough that was used during the Middle Ages.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin carrūca.

parole.significato: A load: various English units of weight or volume based upon standardized cartloads of certain commodities.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin carrus (“load”). Doublet of car and horse.

parole.significato: A member of a Christian contemplative order of monks founded by Bruno of Cologne (St Bruno) in 1084.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Carthusianus, from Cart(h)usia, Latinization of Old French Chartrouse, a region near Grenoble where the order was founded, now Chartreuse; from Late Latin Catorissium, Cantourisa, Caturissium, Chatrousse, probably ultimately from Gaulish *Katurīx (literally “battle-king”). parole.significato: A medieval manuscript register containing full or excerpted transcriptions of important documents, especially of origin…
parole.testo: From Middle English cartulari, borrowed from Medieval Latin chartulārium. Doublet of khaltura.

parole.significato: The notional area of land able to be farmed in a year by a team of 8 oxen pulling a carruca plow, usually reckoned at 1…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin carūcāta (“ploughland”), from Latin carūca (“chariot; coach; carruca”). Compare French charrue (“plough”).

parole.significato: The office of a castellan, the lordship of a castle.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin castellania, from Latin castellānus. Doublet of chatellany.

parole.significato: castle-like: built or shaped like a castle.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin castellātus (“fortified” “made into a castle”), from castellum (“little fortification, castle”) + -ātus (forming participial adjectives). By surface analysis, Latin castellum + -ate (adjective-forming suffix) or castle + -ate.

parole.significato: The district of a castle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin castellātus. By surface analysis, castle + -ate (forming nouns denoting a rank or office, the concrete charge of this office).

parole.significato: Castle-like: built or shaped like a castle; usually, specifically, having castellations (crenellations).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin castellātus (“fortified, castellate”) + -ed (forming past participles). Equivalent to the past participle of castellate but attested earlier than other uses of the verb.

parole.significato: Synonym of enclosed, when used for fountains, cisterns, &c.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin castellum (“cistern”).

parole.significato: Inflammation of a mucous membrane.
parole.testo: From Middle English catarre, from Medieval Latin catarrus, from Late Latin catarrhus, from Ancient Greek κατάρροος (katárrhoos), which is derived from καταρρέω (katarrhéō, “to flow down”), which is composed of κατά (katá, “down”) and ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”).

parole.significato: A series of related items.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin catena, from Latin catēna (“chain”). Doublet of chain.

parole.testo: Recorded since the 16th century; from the masculine plural of Medieval Latin Catharī (“Pure (ones)”), from the masculine plural of Byzantine Greek καθαροί (katharoí, “Pure (ones)”), from the masculine singular of Byzantine Greek καθαρός (katharós, “Pure (one)”), from Ancient Greek καθαρός (katharós,

parole.significato: promulgated ex cathedra; authoritative.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cathedrāticus, from Latin cathedra + -ticus.

parole.significato: The jurisdiction of an Armenian catholicos.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin catholicatus.

parole.significato: A supposed universal remedy.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, via Medieval Latin from Ancient Greek καθολικόν (katholikón, “that which is universal”), the neuter substantive form of καθολικός (katholikós).

parole.significato: The jurisdiction of a catholicos.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin catholicatus.

parole.significato: Tapering into a long, tail-like extension at the apex.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin caudātus, from Classical Latin cauda (“tail”) + -ātus; see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The property of having a caudate extension or tail.
parole.testo: From the Medieval Latin caudātus, from the Classical Latin cauda (“tail”).

parole.significato: The effect of a cause.
parole.testo: First attested in 1652; borrowed from Medieval Latin causātus, perfect passive participle of causō (“to cause”), see -ate (noun-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Serving to caution or warn; admonitory
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin cautiōnārius.

parole.significato: (of an elective franchise, especially in the nineteenth century) dependent on or proportional to a poll tax (cense) or…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin censitarius, from Latin censere (“assess (for tax)”). Compare French censitaire, Spanish and Italian censitario.

parole.significato: Any of the flowering plants in or formerly in the genus Centaurium.
parole.testo: From Middle English centaure, from Old English centaurie, from Medieval Latin centaurēa, centauria, from Latin centaurēum, centaurion, from Ancient Greek κενταύρειον (kentaúreion, “several plants related to Centaurea”), from κένταυρος (kéntauros, “centaur”) (due to the mythological discovery of its

parole.significato: Earwax.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin caerūmen, from cera + -men. The appearance of the u is unexplained, but may have been influenced by words like albūmen and bitūmen.

parole.significato: To depict someone or something a particular way (often negative).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin charactērizō, from Ancient Greek χαρακτηρίζω (kharaktērízō, “to designate by a characteristic mark”), from χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr, “a mark, character”). By surface analysis, character + -ize.

parole.significato: A group of singers and dancers in a theatrical performance or religious festival who commented on the main performance…
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Medieval Latin chorus (“church choir”), Latin chorus (“group of dancers and singers; dance”), from Ancient Greek χορός (khorós, “group of dancers and singers, choir, chorus; dance accompanied by song; round dance”); The verb is derived from the noun. Doublet of choir, chore

parole.significato: A mixture of oil and balm, consecrated for use as an anointing fluid in certain Christian ceremonies, especially confir…
parole.testo: From Middle English crisme, from Late Old English crisma, from Medieval Latin crisma, from Ecclesiastical Latin chrisma, from Ancient Greek χρῖσμα (khrîsma, “anointing”, “unction”), from χρίω (khríō, “anoint”).

parole.significato: Part of a church set aside for the rite of confirmation.
parole.testo: From Middle English crismatorie, from Medieval Latin chrismatōrium, from chrisma, crisma (“chrism”).

parole.significato: A Christogram.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin crismon (New Latin chrismus, chrismum, chrismos), of uncertain origin. In the 18th century adopted in German as Chrismon or Chrismum, plural Chrismen. parole.significato: A fixed vaulted canopy over a Christian altar, supported on four columns.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin cibōrium (“drinking-cup”), from Ancient Greek κιβώριον (kibṓrion, “the Egyptian water-lily’s cupulate seed pod”, or “a drinking-cup fashioned therefrom”). Doublet of cimborio.

parole.significato: Treasures; things considered valuable.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cimelia, cimilia, from Ancient Greek κειμήλῐᾰ (keimḗlĭă), plural of κειμήλῐον (keimḗlĭon, “something stored or saved up; treasure; heirloom”), from κεῖμαι (keîmai, “to lie; to be laid up”).

parole.significato: To move around something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin circumgȳrō; equivalent to circum- + gyrate.

parole.significato: Characterised by circumlocution; overly wordy
parole.testo: From circumlocution + -ory; compare Medieval Latin circumlocūtōrius from Classical Latin circumlocūtiō.

parole.significato: One who studies or works with the civil law.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin civilista, from Latin cīvīlis (“civil (law)”), on the pattern of Medieval Latin canonista (“canonist”), from Latin canōn (“rule”).

parole.significato: The process of cogitating; contemplation, deliberation, reflection, meditation.
parole.testo: Latinism, likely a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin cogitatio, cogitationis, possibly influenced by or displacing an earlier doublet of cogitacion inherited from Middle English cogitacioun, from an Old French cogitaciun, from Vulgar Latin cōgitātiō, cōgitātiōnem; compare Middle French cogitatiu

parole.significato: Relating to the part of mental functions that deals with logic, as opposed to affective which deals with emotions.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cognitīvus, from Latin cognitus, perfect passive participle of cognōscō (“to get to know”) + -īvus (adjective suffix).

parole.significato: A large theatre, cinema, or stadium.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin coliseum, from Latin Colosseum, from neuter of colosseus (“gigantic”), from Ancient Greek κολοσσιαῖος (kolossiaîos), from κολοσσός (kolossós, “giant statue”). See also: w:Colosseum § Name on Wikipedia.

parole.significato: Synonym of collectarium.
parole.testo: Derived from Medieval Latin collectarium + -ary.

parole.significato: A student (or a former student) of a college
parole.testo: From Middle English collegian, from Medieval Latin collēgiānus.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to a college, or college students; collegial.
parole.testo: From Middle English collegiate, from Medieval Latin collēgiātus (“colleague”), from collēgium (“community, group”).

parole.significato: A syrupy solution of nitrocellulose (pyroxylin) in alcohol and ether that evaporates on a surface to form a clear elast…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin collodium, from Ancient Greek κολλώδης (kollṓdēs, “sticky”).

parole.significato: The shared right to graze animals on the same pasture.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin compāscuitās, from compāscuus + -itās.

parole.significato: Being complacent; a feeling of contentment or satisfaction; complacency.
parole.testo: From late Middle English complacence, from Medieval Latin complacentia, from Latin complaceō (“to please”).

parole.significato: A payment of amends or to acquire a certain privilege, (universities) a tuition fee.
parole.testo: Originally from an obsolete sense of composition, “payment to settle an obligation”, from Medieval Latin compositiō (“payment made in amends or settlement”), see citations; compare legal sense of compound, “settle with a smaller payment than the claim”.
