parole.significato: Someone who vouches for another person's innocence, trustworthiness etc.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin compurgator or Middle French compurgateur, from Latin compurgō (“to purify”).

parole.significato: concentrated
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin/New Latin concentrātus, perfect passive participle of concentrō (“concentate”). See Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to concepts or mental conception.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin conceptuālis, from Latin conceptus, perfect passive participle of concipiō (“take hold of; conceive”); see concept and -al.

parole.significato: A surface of revolution formed by rotating a segment of a line around another line that intersects the first line.
parole.testo: From Middle English cone (“corner, angle”) and conoun (“cone”), from Medieval Latin cōnus, cōnon (“cone, wedge, peak”), from Ancient Greek κῶνος (kônos, “cone, spinning top, pine cone”). Reinforced by Middle French cone, from the same Graeco-Latin source.

parole.significato: The percentage of the surface of a culture dish that is covered by adherent cells
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cōnfluentia. Doublet of confluence.

parole.significato: A clear mucous membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelid and the exposed surface of the eyeball or sclera.
parole.testo: From 1540s late Middle English, borrowing from Medieval Latin conjūnctīva (“serving to connect, connective”, feminine), ellipsis of membrāna conjūnctīva (“conjunctive membrane”).

parole.significato: To connote; to suggest or designate (something) as additional or representative; to imply.
parole.testo: First attested in 1596; borrowed from Medieval Latin connotātus, perfect passive participle of connotō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix). Doublet of connote.

parole.significato: A meaning of a word or phrase that is suggested or implied, as opposed to a denotation, or literal meaning. A character…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin connotātiō, from connotō (“to mark in addition”), from Latin con- (“together, with”) + notō (“to note”); equivalent to connote + -ation.

parole.significato: To signify beyond its literal or principal meaning.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin connotō (“signify beyond literal meaning”), from com- (“together”), + notō (“mark”).

parole.significato: Having the quality of preserving from loss, decay, or injury.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cōnservātōrius directly and via French conservatoire, from cōnservāre (“to conserve, to preserve”) + -torius (“-atory: forming related adjectives”) and/or conservator (“conservator, preserver, protector”) + -ius (“-y: forming related adjectives”).

parole.significato: A medicine, especially a magical preservative.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cōnservātōrium directly and via French conservatoire and Italian conservatorio, from cōnservātus (“conserved, preserved”) + -ōrium (“-ory: forming related nouns”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a consistory.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cōnsistōriālis.

parole.significato: To cause constipation in, render costive.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested circa 1425, in Middle English, the verb in 1541; inherited from Middle English constipat(e) (“constipated”), borrowed Medieval Latin cōnstīpātus (“constipated”) (or through its Old French equivalent constipé), perfect passive participle of Medieval Latin cōnstīpō (“to

parole.significato: A state of the bowels in which the evacuations are infrequent and difficult, or the intestines become filled with harde…
parole.testo: First attested in the beginning of the 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English constipacioun, borrowed from Medieval Latin constīpātiō or its Old French equivalent, from cōnstīpō + -tiō. By surface analysis, constipate + -ion.

parole.significato: A person who, or thing that, constructs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin cōnstrūctor, from Latin cōnstruō + Medieval Latin -or. By surface analysis, construct + -or.

parole.significato: A ritual book containing the forms and ceremonies used in the services of a particular monastery, cathedral or religiou…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cōnsuetudinārius, from cōnsuētūdō (oblique stem cōnsuētūdin-) + -ārius, from cōnsuēscō + -tūdō, from con- + suēscō. By surface analysis, consuetude + -ary.

parole.significato: From the same time period, coexistent in time; contemporaneous.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin contemporārius, from Latin con- (“with, together”) + temporārius, an adjective derived from tempus (“time”).

parole.significato: Contiguous, touching.
parole.testo: Middle English contiguat(e), borrowed from Medieval Latin contiguātus, participial adjective from contiguor (“to be contiguous”), from contiguus; see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To dispute, to argue about (something).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin contrōvertere, from Latin contrō- (“against”) + vertere (“to turn”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a convent or convent life; cloistered, monastic.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin conventuālis, from Latin conventus (“convent”).

parole.significato: Of the same rank; equal.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin coōrdinātus, perfect passive participle of coōrdinō (“arrange together”), from co- + ōrdinō, equivalent to co- + ordinate. See -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more. See also ordain and ordinate.

parole.significato: To place in the same order or rank.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin coōrdinātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more. Compare French coordonner.

parole.significato: A long, loose cloak worn by a priest, deacon, or bishop when presiding over a ceremony other than the Mass.
parole.testo: From Middle English cope, from Medieval Latin cāpa (“cape”) Doublet of cap, cape, and chape.

parole.significato: Any of various metallic sulphates formed from the reaction of sulfur with iron, zinc, or copper, especially (alchemy) s…
parole.testo: From Middle English coperas, coperose (“any metallic sulfate”), from Medieval Latin cuprosa directly or via Old French coperose, from Medieval Latin aqua cuprosa (“cupreous water”), from Latin cuprum (“copper”) + -osa (“-ose: forming related adjectives”). Fanciful derivations from cupreous terms inv

parole.significato: jointly or mutually responsive: exchanging
parole.testo: Formed as: correspons- (perfect passive participial stem of the Medieval Latin correspondeō) + -ive; compare responsive.

parole.significato: The study of the physical universe, its structure, dynamics, origin and evolution, and fate.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cosmologia, from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “world”) + -λογία (-logía, “treating of”), combination form of -λόγος (-lógos, “one who speaks (in a certain manner)”). By surface analysis, cosmo- + -logy.

parole.significato: A surplice, in England and America usually one shorter and less full than the ordinary surplice and with short sleeves,…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cotta (“clerical tunic”).

parole.significato: The ruler of a county palatine.
parole.testo: Calque of Medieval Latin comes palātīnus.

parole.significato: sciatic (relating to the hip)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin or Late Latin coxalis, from Latin coxa. By surface analysis, cox- + -al.

parole.significato: Forms terms relating to the cranium (skull).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin crānium, borrowed from Ancient Greek κρᾱνῐ́ον (krānĭ́on), from *κρᾱν- (*krān-) + -ῐ́ον (-ĭ́on).

parole.significato: That part of the skull consisting of the bones enclosing the brain, but not including the bones of the face or jaw.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin crānium (“skull”), from Ancient Greek κρᾱνίον (krāníon, “skull”). By surface analysis, crani- + -um.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or serving as an introduction or recommendation (to someone).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin crēdentiālis (“giving authority”), from Latin crēdentia (“trust”).

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Croatia; a person of Croatian ethnicity.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin Croata, borrowed from Proto-Slavic *xъrvatъ (“Croat”), the Croatian autonym. It, in turn, is probably of non-Slavic origin: probably from an Iranian or Germanic language. First attested in 1585. Doublet of cravat.

parole.significato: A cultivator of crocus or saffron; a dealer in saffron.
parole.testo: From a Medieval Latin *crocarius, derivative of Latin crocus, from Ancient Greek κρόκος (krókos).

parole.significato: Glove; mitten
parole.testo: From Middle English cuffe, coffe (“glove, mitten”), of obscure origin. Perhaps from Old English cuffie (“hood, cap”), from Medieval Latin cofia, cofea, cuffa, cuphia (“helmet, headdress, hood, cap”), from Frankish *kuf(f)ja (“headdress”), from Proto-West Germanic *kuffju, from Proto-Germanic *kupjō

parole.significato: Of a heavenly body, to be at the highest point, reach its greatest altitude.
parole.testo: First attested in 1647; borrowed from Medieval Latin culminātus, perfect passive participle of culminō (“to crown”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin culmen (“peak, highest point”, oblique stem culmin-) + -ō (verb-forming suffix), older form columen (“top, summit”), from Proto-Italic *kol

parole.significato: To grow plants, notably crops.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cultivātus, perfect passive participle of cultivō (“till, cultivate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more), from cultīvus (“tilled”), from Latin cultus, perfect passive participle of colō (“till, cultivate”), which comes from earlier *quelō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (

parole.significato: The art or act of cultivating (improvement of land for or by agriculture), as:
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cultivātus, perfect passive participle of cultivō, + -ion, or Middle French cultivation. By surface analysis, cultivate + -ion.

parole.significato: A member of a nomadic Turkic people of central Asia who ruled parts of Eurasia and Eastern Europe in the Middle Ages.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Cumani, from Byzantine Greek Κουμάνοι (Koumánoi), perhaps ultimately from the name of the Kuma River.

parole.significato: The superintendent of the engravers of dies for making coins.
parole.testo: From cuneātor, Medieval Latin equivalent of Old French coigneur (“coiner”).

parole.significato: An assistant rector or vicar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin cūrātus (“one who has been curated, a curate”), a substantivation of the perfect passive participle of cūrō. Doublet of curato. Equivalent to cure + -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Money or other items used to facilitate transactions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin currentia. By surface analysis, current + -cy.

parole.significato: In accordance with, or established by, custom or common usage.
parole.testo: From Middle English custumary, from Medieval Latin custumarius. By surface analysis, custom + -ary.

parole.significato: The main justice of the peace in a given county of England, Wales or Ireland.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin custos rotulorum, from Latin custōs (“custos, keeper”) + genitive plural of rotulus (“roll”).

parole.significato: Denoting an alphabet devised for writing the Old Church Slavonic liturgical language, and its adaptations used for seve…
parole.testo: From the name Cyril + -ic, from Medieval Latin Cȳrillus, from Ancient Greek Κῡ́ρῐλλος (Kū́rĭllos), denoting Saint Cyril, who devised a predecessor to the Cyrillic script, the Glagolitic alphabet, and whose students later devised the Cyrillic script itself.

parole.significato: A kind of mead made with apples.
parole.testo: From Middle English ciser (“alcoholic beverage of great strength and potency”), from Medieval Latin sīcera, from Ancient Greek σίκερα (síkera), from Hebrew שֵׁכָר (šēḵār). Doublet of cider.

parole.significato: A bulbous plant of the genus Narcissus, with yellow flowers and a trumpet shaped corona, especially Narcissus pseudonar…
parole.testo: Variant of Middle English affodill (“ramson”), from Medieval Latin affodillus, from Latin asphodelus, from Ancient Greek ἀσφόδελος (asphódelos), of Pre-Greek origin. The initial d- is perhaps from merging of the article in Dutch de affodil, the Netherlands being a source for bulbs (compare adder, ap

parole.significato: An ornate silk fabric originating from Damascus.
parole.testo: From Middle English damaske, from Medieval Latin damascus, named after the city Damascus, where the fabric was originally made.

parole.significato: Synonym of Danish.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dānicus.

parole.significato: The servant that brings the meat to the table at a meal.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin dapifer, from Latin daps (“feast”) + -fer (“bearer”).

parole.significato: The dignity of a dauphin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin delphīnātus. By surface analysis, dauphin + -ate (forms nouns denoting a rank or office). Doublet of Delphinate, Dauphiny, and Dauphiné.

parole.significato: The act of conquering or subjugation in war.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēbellātiō (“total defeat”), from dēbellō (“conquer, subjugate”).

parole.significato: A group of parishes over which a dean presides; a deanery.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin decānātus, from Latin decānus. Equivalent to Latin decānus + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, here the concrete charge of it). Compare dean.

parole.significato: Of or related to a tithing.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin decēnārius, from decēna (“a tithing”) + -ārius (“-ary”).

parole.significato: To roast (a salt or mineral) until it stops crackling in the fire.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēcrepitātus, perfect passive participle of dēcrepitō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin dē- + crepitō.

parole.significato: To misappropriate funds; to embezzle.
parole.testo: First attested in the 1530s, in the sense “to lop off”; borrowed from Medieval Latin dēfalcātus, perfect passive participle of dēfalcō (“to cut or lop off”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin dē (“off”) + falx (“sickle, scythe, pruning hook”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of cancelling part of a claim by deducting a smaller claim which the claimant owes to the defendant.
parole.testo: Late 15th century, from Medieval Latin dēfalcātiōnem, accusative singular of dēfalcātiō (literally “cutting off, lopping off with a sickle”), nominalization of dēfalcō, from Latin dē (“off”) + falx (“sickle, scythe, pruning hook”), from which also English falcate (“sickle-shaped”). By surface analys

parole.significato: The killing of a deity; godslaughter.
parole.testo: Merged from Medieval Latin deicīdium and Medieval Latin deicīda.

parole.significato: Godlike.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin deifōrmis (literally “godlike”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a dauphin
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin delphīnālis, from delphīnus + -ālis.

parole.significato: To turn into a demon.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin daemonizō, from daemon + -izō. Compare Ancient Greek δαιμονίζομαι (daimonízomai, “to be possessed by a demon”), from δαίμων (daímōn, “demon”). By surface analysis, demon + -ize.

parole.significato: To withdraw, or cause to withdraw, from one's country; to banish or expatriate.
parole.testo: From de- + Latin patria (“fatherland”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix) or an altered borrowing from Medieval Latin dispatriō.

parole.significato: Having stunted growth
parole.testo: From Middle English depauperat (“impoverished”), from Medieval Latin depauperātus (“impoverished”), past participle of depauperō (“to impoverish”), itself from Latin de- + pauperō (“to impoverish”), from pauper (“poor”). Equivalent to de- + pauper + -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Cognate with Ital

parole.significato: A place where something is deposited, as for storage, safekeeping, or preservation.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin dēpositōrium, from Latin dēpositum, past participle of dēpōnō. By surface analysis, deposit + -ory.

parole.significato: To cut, as with a scythe; to mow.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Medieval Latin dēsecātus, a variant of dēsectus, the perfect passive participle of dēsecō (“to cut off”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A deserted island, an uninhabited island, especially one in the tropics and (now frequently misunderstood as) a small a…
parole.testo: From the former sense of desert to mean deserted (“uninhabited”), particularly common on Spanish and Portuguese maps during the Age of Exploration as isla desierta, ilha deserta, and Medieval Latin isla deserta (“uninhabited island”). Now frequently misunderstood as simply desert (“dry, arid locatio

parole.significato: Capable of being designated; designatable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēsignābilis, from dēsignō (“to indicate, designate”).

parole.significato: consisting of desinences or grammatical endings; terminal
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin dēsinentia + -al. Compare French désinentiel.

parole.significato: To shut up, as in a desk; to treasure.
parole.testo: From Middle English deske, desque, from Medieval Latin desca, modified from Old Italian desco, from Latin discus. Doublet of dais, disc, discus, dish, disk, and diskos. See also German Tisch, "table".

parole.significato: Causing damage or harm.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin *dētrīmentālis, from Latin dētrīmentum (“harm”), from dēterō (“to rub off, wear”), from dē- (“down, away”) + terō (“to rub or grab”).

parole.significato: Waste or misapplication of the assets of a deceased person by an executor or administrator; devastation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēvastāvit (“he has wasted”), from dēvastāre, from dēvastō (“to devastate, lay waste”), from de- + vastāre (from vastō (“to devastate, lay waste, ravage”), from vastus (“deserted, wasted”), from Proto-Indo-European *weh₂st- (“empty; wasted”)).

parole.significato: Transparent or translucent; allowing light to pass through; capable of being seen through.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin diaphanus, from Ancient Greek διαφανής (diaphanḗs), from δια- (dia-, “through”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine, appear”).

parole.significato: A reference work listing words or names from one or more languages, usually ordered alphabetically, explaining each ter…
parole.testo: From Middle English dixionare, a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin dictiōnārium, from Latin dictiōnārius, from dictiō (“a speaking”), from dictus, perfect past participle of dīcō (“to speak”) + -ārium (“room, place”). By surface analysis, diction + -ary.

parole.significato: A regulated diet that excludes or constrains certain types of food, especially for health reasons; also, a book or simi…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin diētārium (“book prescribing diet”), from Latin diaeta (“diet”).

parole.significato: A light strong fabric with woven stripes or squares.
parole.testo: From earlier dimite, from Middle English demit, demyt, from Medieval Latin dimitum, from Byzantine Greek δίμιτον (dímiton), from Ancient Greek δίμιτος (dímitos, “of double thread”).

parole.significato: A list of names, addresses etc, of specific classes of people or organizations, often in alphabetical order or in some…
parole.testo: From Middle English directorie, dyrectorye, from Medieval Latin dīrēctōrium. By surface analysis, direct + -ory. Doublet of directorium. The political sense is a semantic loan from French directoire.

parole.significato: Having to do with discipline, or with the imposition of discipline.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin disciplinarius, from Latin disciplina (“instruction, teaching, field of study, habit”).

parole.significato: Cheerless, dreary.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin discōnsōlātus (“comfortless”), from dis- (“away”) + cōnsōlātus (“consoled”).

parole.significato: To free from blame or the imputation of a fault; to exonerate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin disculpātus, perfect passive participle of disculpō (“to disculpate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dis- (“off”, denoting the ending of an action) + culpō (“to blame”), from culpa (“fault”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of disculp.

parole.significato: To make dissimilar or unlike.
parole.testo: First attested in 1841; borrowed from Medieval Latin dissimilātus, perfect passive participle of dissimilō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), hypercorrected form of Classical Latin dissimulō, from dis- + simulō, from similis (“similar, the same as”); the vocalism was perhaps influenced by assimilate,

parole.significato: Immoderate, excessive.
parole.testo: First attested in 1398, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English distemperat(e), borrowed from Medieval Latin distemperātus (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from dis- + temperātus, perfect passive participle of temperō (“to temperate oneself, show restraint”).

parole.significato: To run apart; to separate; to tend into different directions.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin dīvergō (“bend away from, go in a different direction”), from Latin dī- + vergō (“bend”).

parole.significato: The act, or the result, of diversifying.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin diversificatiō, from diversificātus, past participle of diversificō (“diversify”), from Latin diversus (“turned in different ways”) + faciō (“make, do”). By surface analysis, diverse + -ification.

parole.significato: A tactic used to draw attention away from the real threat or action.
parole.testo: From Middle English diversion, dyversioun, from Medieval Latin diversiō, from Latin divertō (“to divert”); see divert.

parole.significato: A postgraduate aiming to receive a doctorate; a Ph.D. student.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin doctōrandus. Doublet of doctorandus.

parole.significato: Something transposed from a thought to a document; the written account of an idea.
parole.testo: From document + -ation or Medieval Latin documentātio.

parole.significato: An animal or plant that has been domesticated.
parole.testo: First attested in 1860; borrowed from Medieval Latin domesticātus (“domesticated”), see Etymology 1 and -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Jesus Christ as Lord.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English dominical (“(adjective) of or pertaining to the Lord’s day or Sunday; (noun) a book containing the liturgy for Sunday (?)”), borrowed from Medieval Latin dominicālis (“of or pertaining to Sunday, dominical”), from Latin dominicus (“of or belonging to a lord or master; (

parole.significato: One of a group of Christians in fourth-century North Africa who broke away as a group after opposing the appointment of…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Dōnātista, from Dōnātus, one of their leaders.

parole.significato: With respect to, or concerning the side in which the backbone is located, or the analogous side of an invertebrate.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English dorsal/dorsale, borrowing from Medieval Latin dorsālis (“of or relating to the back”), from dorsum (“the back”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix); equivalent to dorsum + -al.

parole.significato: An expression of praise to God, especially a short hymn sung as part of a Christian worship service.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin doxologia, from Ancient Greek δοξολογία (doxología, “a praising”), from δοξολόγος (doxológos, “giving or uttering praise”), from δόξα (dóxa, “glory, honor, repute”), from δοκέω (dokéō, “to think, expect”).

parole.significato: A legendary being with a human head, and sometimes also human arms and a torso, and the rest of the body of a snake.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin dracontopedis, draconcopedis, from Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn, “serpent”) + πούς (poús, “foot, leg”).

parole.significato: A kind of feudal free tenant with military duties, mentioned in the Domesday Book.
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Medieval Latin drengus, from Middle English dreng (“warrior, retainer”) or its source, Old English drenġ (“warrior, soldier”), from Proto-West Germanic *drangī, from Proto-Germanic *drangijaz, cognate to Old Norse drengr.

parole.significato: Arranged, regular combat between two private persons, often over a matter of honor.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin duellum (“fight between two men, duel”), itself from Old Latin duellum (“war, fight”), which survived in Classical Latin as a rare byform of bellum and was later reinterpreted as “duel” by unetymological association with duo (“two”). May have entered English through Middle French

parole.significato: The first part of the small intestine, starting at the lower end of the stomach and extending to the jejunum.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin duodēnum digitōrum (“space of twelve digits”) in reference to its length, from duodēnī (“twelve each”) + digitōrum, genitive plural of digitus (“finger; toe; digit”).

parole.significato: A form of bell used in some medieval clocks.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin dupla.

parole.significato: The tough and inflexible outermost of the three layers of the meninges, enveloping the brain and spinal cord.
parole.testo: First attested c. 1400, borrowing from Medieval Latin dūra māter (literally “firm, strict mother”), ellipsis of dūra māter cerebrī (literally “hard mother of the brain”), calque of Arabic أُمّ الدِّمَاغ الصَفِيقَة (ʔumm al-ddimāḡ aṣ-ṣafīqa, literally “thick mother of the brain”).

parole.significato: A form of the letter e modified by the addition of a diacritical “tail”: ⟨ę⟩.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ē caudāta (literally “tailed e”).

parole.significato: Of a sound or sound waves: to reflect off a surface and return; to reverberate or resound.
parole.testo: From Middle English eccho, ecco, echo, ekko, from Medieval Latin ēccō, from Latin ēchō, from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ), from ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound”). Possibly from the same Proto-Indo-European root as sough.

parole.significato: A person who edits or makes changes to documents.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ēditor, from Late Latin ēditor, from ēditus, perfect passive participle of ēdō (“give out, put forth, publish”).

parole.significato: To sweeten.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ēdulcōrō. Compare French édulcorer.

parole.significato: Gushy; unrestrained, extravagant or excessive (in emotional expression).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin effūsīvus, 1660s.

parole.significato: Relating to charity, alms, or almsgiving.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin eleēmosynārius (“alms dispenser”), from Late Latin eleēmosyna (“alms”), from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē, “alms”), from ἐλεήμων (eleḗmōn, “merciful”) + -σῠ́νη (-sŭ́nē, “suffix denoting an abstract noun”). Compare Italian elemosina.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or being an element (as opposed to a compound).
parole.testo: From Middle English elementall, from Medieval Latin elementālis; compare Old French elementel. By surface analysis, element + -al.

parole.significato: A liquid which converts lead to gold.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin elixir (“philosopher's stone”), from Arabic اَلْإِكْسِير (al-ʔiksīr, “philosopher's stone”), from Ancient Greek ξηρίον (xēríon, “powder for drying wounds”), from ξηρός (xērós, “dry”).

parole.significato: The act of eluding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ēlūsiō.

parole.significato: To deprive of virile or procreative power; to castrate, to geld.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ēmasculātus, perfect passive participle of ēmasculō (“to emasculate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ē(x)- (“out, from, apart”) + masculus (“male, masculine”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), further from mās (“a man, a male”) + -culus (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: Deprived of virility or vigor; unmanned, weak.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ēmasculātus (more at Etymology 1), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The fruit of Emblica officinalis (now Phyllanthus emblica, the Indian gooseberry, once used as a remedy against dysente…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin emblicus, from Arabic أَمْلَج (ʔamlaj), from Sanskrit आमलक (āmalaka). Doublet of amla.

parole.significato: To rub (a diseased part) with a moistened or liquid substance, usually an oil, on a cloth or sponge.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin embrocatus, past participle of Late Latin embrocare, from embrocha, from Ancient Greek ἐμβροχή (embrokhḗ, “lotion, fomentation”).

parole.significato: In the reproductive cycle, the stage after the fertilization of the egg that precedes the development into a fetus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin embryō, from Ancient Greek ἔμβρυον (émbruon, “fetus”), from ἐν (en, “in-”) + βρύω (brúō, “to grow, swell”).

parole.significato: Embryonic.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin embryon, from Ancient Greek ἔμβρυον (émbruon, “newborn animal, embryo”).

parole.significato: To express support or approval, especially officially or publicly; to give an endorsement.
parole.testo: Alteration influenced by Medieval Latin indorsare of Middle English endosse, from Old French endosser (“to put on the back”), from Latin dossum, alternative form of dorsum (“back”), from which also dorsal (“of the back”). That is, the ‘r’ was dropped in Latin dossum, which developed into Old French

parole.significato: That which has a distinct existence as an individual unit, often used for organizations which have no physical form.
parole.testo: From the Medieval Latin entitās, from ēns (“being”) (stem: ent-) + -tās (compare essentia), see there for more information.

parole.significato: A particular period of history, or of a person's life, especially one considered noteworthy or remarkable.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin epocha, from Ancient Greek ἐποχή (epokhḗ, “a check, cessation, stop, pause, epoch of a star, i.e., the point at which it seems to halt after reaching the highest, and generally the place of a star; hence, a historical epoch”), from ἐπέχω (epékhō, “to hold in, check”), from ἐπι- (

parole.significato: To perform equiparation; to transfer attributes from one object or concept to another.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin aequiparātus, past participle of aequiparō (“put on a level with, compare”), from aequus (“equal”) + parō (“place”).

parole.significato: The transfer or imputation of attributes from one object or concept to another; the drawing of an equivalence between t…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin aequiparātiō, from aequiparō (“put on a level with, compare”) + -tiō (noun suffix), from aequus (“equal”) + parō (“place”). Equivalent to equiparate + -ion.

parole.significato: To speak using double meaning; to speak ambiguously, unclearly or doubtfully, with intent to deceive; to vacillate in o…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English equivocaten, from Medieval Latin aequivocātus, perfect passive participle of aequivocō (“to be called by the same name”), from Late Latin aequivocus (“ambiguous, equivocal”). Compare French équivoque.

parole.significato: An exchange student taking part in an Erasmus Programme.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Erasmus. The EU student exchange programme is named after Erasmus of Rotterdam, and also a backronym for “European [Community] Action Scheme for the Mobility of University Students”.

parole.significato: A rabbit.
parole.testo: Coined in a 1995 episode of the animated TV show The Simpsons named "Lisa's Wedding", in which a Renaissance fair sideshow falsely promotes a normal rabbit as "a horse with the head of a rabbit and the body of a rabbit". Possibly inspired by fanciful names for creatures from Medieval Latin (e.g. bas

parole.significato: A book of etymologies.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin etymologicon.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Gubbio.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Eugubīnus.

parole.significato: A eulogy.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin eulogium, apparently from a confusion between ēlogium and eulogia. Doublet of eulogy.

parole.significato: The act or state of vanishing away; disappearance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ēvānēscentia.

parole.significato: Of or providing evidence.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ēvidentiālis, from Latin ēvidentia + -ālis.

parole.significato: Resembling an exclamation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin exclāmātōrius.

parole.significato: The act of exculpating from alleged fault or crime.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin exculpātiō. By surface analysis, exculpate + -ion.

parole.significato: Tending to excuse or clear of wrongdoing.
parole.testo: From exculpate + -ory (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of or pertaining to, serving for’). Exculpate is derived from Medieval Latin exculpātus, perfect passive participle of exculpō (“to free from blame, exculpate”), from ex- (prefix meaning ‘out, away’) + culpa (“defect, fault; crime”) (u

parole.significato: A female person who executes or carries out something.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English executrice, executrix (“female executor; administrator of the law; wielder of fate”), from Medieval Latin execūtrīx (possibly through Anglo-Norman *executrice) from execūtor, exsecūtor (“accomplisher, performer; prosecutor, revenger”), + Latin -trīx (suffix forming feminine

parole.significato: The point of complete depletion, of the state of being used up.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin exhaustiō, from exhauriō. Surface analysis: exhaust + -ion.

parole.significato: Including every possible element: fully comprehensive.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin exhaustīvus. By surface analysis, exhaust + -ive.

parole.significato: To dig out of the ground; to take out of a place of burial; to disinter.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin exhumō, from Latin ex- + humō (“to bury”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Exeter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Exonia, the Latin name for Exeter which appears in the Liber Exoniensis (1086), + -an. See its adjectival form Exoniensis.

parole.significato: To drive out (an evil spirit) from a person, place or thing, especially by an incantation or prayer.
parole.testo: From Middle English exorcisen, exorzisen, from Medieval Latin exorcizō, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκίζω (exorkízō, “to banish an evil spirit; bind by oath”), from ἐξ (ex) + ὅρκος (hórkos). Compare Old French exorciser.

parole.significato: The minor order of exorcists.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin exorcistātus.

parole.significato: Living outside of one's own country.
parole.testo: The verb is first attested in 1787, the adjective and noun in 1812; borrowed from Medieval Latin expatriātus, perfect passive participle of expatriō (“to banish”) (see -ate (etymology 1,2 and 3)), from Latin ex- (“out of”) + patria (“native land”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); possibly after French ex

parole.significato: Act of expending or paying out.
parole.testo: From stem of Medieval Latin expenditus, irregular perfect passive participle of expendō (“to weigh, to pay out”), + -ure (“process or result”).

parole.significato: To deprive a person of (their private property) for public use.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin expropriātus.

parole.significato: Outside of something; on the exterior.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English, from Medieval Latin externus (“outward, external”), from exter/exterus (“on the outside, outward”).

parole.significato: To rove.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin extrāvagāt- + English -ate (suffix forming verbs). Extrāvagāt- is the participial stem of extrāvagārī, from Latin extrā (“beyond, outside of”, preposition) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰs (“out”)) + vagārī (the present active infinitive of vagor (“t

parole.significato: Of or affecting the face.
parole.testo: Early 17th century, borrowed from Medieval Latin faciālis (“face-to-face, direct, open”), from faciēs (“form, configuration, figure; face, visage, countenance”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: A person employed to perform all sorts of duties.
parole.testo: Ellipsis of domine fac totum, dominus fac totum /dominus factotum (“absolute ruler; head servant”), from Medieval Latin domine fac tōtum (“O Lord, do everything”), also with substition of nominative dominus for vocative domine.

parole.significato: Capable of making mistakes or being wrong.
parole.testo: From Middle English fallible, from Medieval Latin fallibilis (“liable to err, also deceitful”), from Latin fallere (“to deceive”).

parole.significato: A vernacular paraphrase inserted into Latin liturgy.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin farsa. Doublet of farce.

parole.significato: To favor especially or unduly.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin favorizare.

parole.significato: Feverish, or having a high temperature.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin febrīlis, from Latin febris (“fever”). By surface analysis, Latin febr- + -ile.

parole.significato: Pertaining to an ordinary weekday, rather than a festival or fast.
parole.testo: From Middle English ferial, from Medieval Latin fēriālis, from Latin fēria (“weekday”) (whence the first sense), fēriae (“holidays”) (whence the second).

parole.significato: An estate granted to a vassal by a feudal lord in exchange for service.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin feudum. Doublet of fee, fief, and feoff.

parole.significato: In English law, a writ of execution issued after judgment obtained in a legal action for debt or damages.
parole.testo: From Middle English fieri facias, from Medieval Latin fierī faciās (“thou shouldst cause it to be done”), which is not a normal Classical Latin construction but a calque from Romance causatives from faciō and infinitive (attested since Late Latin).

parole.significato: A fine thread or wire.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin fīlāmentum, from Late Latin fīlō (“to spin, draw out in a long line”), from Latin fīlum (“thread”).

parole.significato: A device which separates a suspended, dissolved, or particulate matter from a fluid, solution, or other substance; any…
parole.testo: From Middle English filtre, from Medieval Latin filtrum (compare also Old French feutre (“felt; filter”)), from Frankish *filtir, from Proto-West Germanic *felt. See felt. Doublet of phin.

parole.significato: Flathe; flan.
parole.testo: From Middle English flathon, probably representing Medieval Latin fladon-, stem form of flado (“a flat-cake”), from Frankish *flaþō (“flat-cake”). Cognate with Middle English flathe (“a flat-cake, flat fish”). More at flathe.

parole.significato: A leaf of a book or manuscript.
parole.testo: From Middle English folio (“leaf of a book”), borrowed from Medieval Latin foliō, Late Latin foliō, Latin foliō, the ablative singular form of Late Latin folium (“leaf or sheet of paper”), Latin folium (“leaf of a plant”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“bloom, flower”). Doublet of fo

parole.significato: Only used in vicar forane and vicariate forane.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin forāneus (“from elsewhere, foreign, non-resident”), from forās (“outdoors”) + -āneus, likely formed by analogy with extrāneus.

parole.significato: An unmarried person who engages in sexual intercourse, especially when considered to be of an illicit or illegal nature.
parole.testo: From Middle English fornicatour, from Medieval Latin fornicātor.

parole.significato: A small fortress.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin fortalitia, from fortis (“strong”). Doublet of fortress.

parole.significato: Synonym of Franciscan: a member of the Order of the Friars Minor.
parole.testo: A calque of Medieval Latin Fratres Minores (“the Lesser Brothers”), both directly and via Old French freres meneurs and Norman freres menures, a name supposedly chosen by St Francis to inculcate humility.

parole.significato: Able to be substituted for something of equal value or utility.
parole.testo: 1765 as noun, 1818 as adjective, from Medieval Latin fungibilis, from Latin fungor (“to perform, discharge a duty”) + -ible (“able to”). Originally a legal term, going back to Roman law: res fungibiles (“replaceable things”).

parole.significato: Forked, branched; divided at one end into parts.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin furcātus (“forked, branched”), from Latin furca (“fork”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Compare French fourchu. The verb was formed by metanalysis or as if from Latin furcō (“to fork”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Having a forked tail
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin furcātus (“forked, branched”), from Latin furca (“fork”) + -cercous.

parole.significato: A (normally) complete range.
parole.testo: 1520s, original sense “lowest note of musical scale”, contraction of Medieval Latin gamma ut, from gamma (“Greek letter, corresponding to the musical note G”) + ut (“first solfège syllable, now replaced by do”). In modern terms, “G do” – the first note of the G scale. Meaning later extended to mean

parole.significato: To bend the knee, as in servitude.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ǵónu From around 1620–1630 from Medieval Latin genūflectō (“to bend the knee”) equivalent to the Latin genū (“knee”) + flectō (“to bend”).

parole.significato: A method of divination using earth or the ground, such as interpreting markings on the ground or how handfuls of dirt l…
parole.testo: From Middle English geomancie, from Medieval Latin geomantia from late Ancient Greek γεωμαντεία (geōmanteía). Equivalent to geo- + -mancy.

parole.significato: A motion of the limbs or body, especially one made to emphasize speech.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin gestūra (“a mode of action”), from Latin gerō (“to bear; (reflexive) bear oneself, behave, act”), past participle gestus. By surface analysis, Latin gest- + -ure.

parole.significato: Grammar, particularly medieval Latin grammar.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin glomeria (“grammar”).

parole.significato: One who writes glosses.
parole.testo: From Middle English glosatour, from Medieval Latin glōsātor, glossātor, from glōsāre, glōssāre (“to gloss”) + Latin -tor (agent suffix).

parole.significato: Deceitful and flattering; toadying.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Gnathōnicus, from Gnathō (genitive Gnathōnis), name of a parasitical character in the Eunuchus of Terence. Gnathō is from Ancient Greek γνάθος (gnáthos, “jaw”), used in the genitive γνάθου (gnáthou, “of a jaw”) to mean “greedy”; hence, a parasite in general.

parole.significato: Proceeding or advancing by small, slow, regular steps or degrees
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin graduālis, from Latin gradus (“step”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰradʰ-, *gʰredʰ- (“to walk, go”). Cognate with Gothic 𐌲𐍂𐌹𐌸𐍃 (griþs, “step, grade”), Bavarian Gritt (“step, stride”).

parole.significato: A student who has completed the requirements for, but has not yet been awarded, a particular degree.
parole.testo: Attested since 1882. From Medieval Latin graduandus, gerundive of graduō (“to graduate”).

parole.significato: A person who is recognized as having completed any of various levels of education.
parole.testo: From Middle English graduat(e) (“(noun) a graduate of a university; (adjective) graduate, having graduated”, also used as the past participle of graduaten (“to graduate”)), borrowed from Medieval Latin graduātus (“graduated, graduate”), perfect passive participle of graduō (“to graduate”) (see -ate

parole.significato: To be recognized by a school or university as having completed the requirements of a degree studied at the institution.
parole.testo: From Middle English graduaten (“to graduate”), from (adjective) graduat(e) (also used as the past participle of graduaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), from Medieval Latin graduātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

parole.significato: Use of Greek words and examples.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin graecismus. Doublet of Grecism.

parole.significato: granular
parole.testo: From Middle English granulous, from Medieval Latin granulōsus.

parole.significato: A horizontal metal grill through which liquid, ash, or small objects can fall, while larger objects cannot.
parole.testo: From Middle English grate, from a Medieval Latin crāta, from a Latin word for a hurdle; or Italian grata, from Latin cratis.

parole.significato: pregnancy
parole.testo: From Middle English gravidacionne, from Medieval Latin gravidātiō.

parole.significato: Having a gray, mottled appearance
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin grīseus, from Proto-West Germanic *grīs (“grey”) (for which compare French gris and German greis) and -eus.

parole.significato: Synonym of guberniya.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin gubernium.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a habit; established as a habit; performed over and over again; recurrent, recurring.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English habitual (“of one's inherent disposition”), from Medieval Latin habituālis (“customary; habitual”), from Latin habitus (“character; disposition; habit; physical or emotional condition; attire, dress”) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationshi

parole.significato: The act of habituating, or accustoming; the state of being habituated.
parole.testo: From Middle English habituacioun, from Medieval Latin habituātio. By surface analysis, habituate + -ion.

parole.significato: The essence of a particular thing that gives it its unique particularity; those qualities that make an individual this…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin haecceitas (“thisness”) coined by Duns Scotus (from haec (“this, these”)) + -ity.

parole.significato: An (early) Arab Muslim.
parole.testo: From Middle English Agarene, from Medieval Latin Agarēnus. By surface analysis, Hagar + -ene. From the belief that Arabs are descendants of Hagar and Abraham.

parole.significato: A kind of basket, usually of wickerwork, and adapted for the packing and carrying of articles; a hamper
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hanaperium (“a large vase”), extended from hanapus (“bowl, cup”). Doublet of hamper.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the German Hanse.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hanseaticus, from hansa, of Germanic origin, from Old High German hansa (“troop, company”), from Proto-West Germanic *hansu (“crowd, company”).

parole.significato: A figure of speech used for emphasis, where two words joined by and are used to express a single complex idea.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin, from Ancient Greek ἕν (hén), stem of εἷς (heîs, “one”) + διά (diá, “through”) + δύο (dúo, “two”), “one [idea] through two [words]”.

parole.significato: heretical
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin haeresiacus (“heretical”).

parole.significato: To denounce as heresy or a heretic.
parole.testo: First attested in 1629; borrowed from Medieval Latin haereticātus, perfect passive participle of haereticō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the ancient Greek Olympian god Hermes.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hermeticus, irregular derivation of Hermes Trismegistus, the god and mythological alchemist, said to possess a magic ability to seal treasure chests so that nothing could access their contents.

parole.significato: A type of root, probably from a plant of the genus Colchicum, as imported and used in Western medicine.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hermodactylus, from Ancient Greek ἑρμοδάκτυλος (hermodáktulos, “Hermes's finger”).

parole.significato: A monk of the Orthodox Catholic Church that engages in noetic prayer.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hesychasta, from ecclesiastical Greek ἡσυχαστής (hēsukhastḗs), from ἡσυχάζειν (hēsukházein, “to be quiet”), from ἥσυχος (hḗsukhos, “quiet”).

parole.significato: Diverse in kind or nature; composed of diverse parts.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin heterogeneus, from Ancient Greek ἑτερογενής (heterogenḗs, “of different kinds”), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”) + γένος (génos, “kind”). Compare hetero- and -ous.

parole.significato: Relating to hidrosis.
parole.testo: From the Medieval Latin hidrōticus, from the Ancient Greek ἱδρωτικός (hidrōtikós), from ἱδρώς (hidrṓs, “sweat”, stem: ἱδρωτ-); by surface analysis, hidr(osis)- + -otic.

parole.significato: One who has high and controlling authority in sacred things; the chief of a sacred order.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hierarcha, from Ancient Greek ἱεράρχης (hierárkhēs) Derived from ἱερός (hierós, “holy”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “ruler”, “leader”). ἱερός from Proto-Hellenic *iherós, from Proto-Indo-European *ish₁ros. There are a number of candidate cognates with this word. Compare Sanskrit इषिर (iṣi

parole.significato: Pertaining to, or in accordance with the theories of, ancient Greek physician and philosopher Hippocrates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Hippocraticus, equivalent to Hippocrates + -ic.

parole.significato: Of the same kind; alike, similar.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin homogeneus, from Ancient Greek ὁμογενής (homogenḗs, “of the same race, family or kind”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”) + γένος (génos, “kind”). Compare homo- (“same”) and -ous (adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: The state of being able to achieve honours; honourableness.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin honōrificābilitūdinitātibus, the ablative and dative plural of honōrificābilitūdinitās (“the state of being able to achieve honours”).

parole.significato: The quality of being honourable; honourableness.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin honōrificābilitūdinitās.

parole.significato: Pertaining to an hour or hours.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hōrārius, from Latin hōra (“hour”).

parole.significato: Synonym of matter, physical substance.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hyle, from Ancient Greek ὕλη (húlē, “wood, matter”), particularly in Aristotle as πρώτη ὕλη (prṓtē húlē, “protomatter, fundamental undifferentiated matter”).

parole.significato: Synonym of physical, material, or base.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hylicus, from Ancient Greek ὑλικός (hulikós, “wooden, material”), from ῡ̔́λη (hū́lē, “wood, matter”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic, forming adjectives”). As a noun, a clipped calque of homo hylicus (“hylic man”).

parole.significato: A collection of hymns; a hymn book.
parole.testo: From Middle English hymnale, from Medieval Latin hymnāle, noun use of neuter of hymnālis.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to hymns.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hymnālis.

parole.significato: A level of veneration higher than dulia but less than latria, properly given to the Virgin Mary only.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hyperdūlīa, from hyper-, from Ancient Greek ὑπέρ (hupér, “above”) + dūlīa, from Ancient Greek δουλείᾱ (douleíā, “slavery”), from δοῦλος (doûlos, “slave”).

parole.significato: legendary asp said to kill people by making them go in an endless sleep or by attacking them in their sleep.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ypnalis, ipnalis, from Ancient Greek ὕπνος (húpnos, “sleep”).

parole.significato: The liquid said to flow in place of blood in the veins of the gods.
parole.testo: Sense 1 (“liquid said to flow in place of blood in the veins of the gods”) is borrowed from Medieval Latin ichor, from Ancient Greek ῑ̓χώρ (īkhṓr, “fluid running through the veins of gods, ichor; watery part of blood, lymph, serum; watery part of milk, whey; gravy; pus; naphtha”); further etymology

parole.significato: The quality or state of being ideal.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ideālitās (“ideality”), from Late Latin ideālis (“ideal”). By surface analysis, ideal + -ity.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being idoneous.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin idōneitās.

parole.significato: The last, and usually the longest, division of the small intestine; the part between the jejunum and large intestine.
parole.testo: Via Medieval Latin from Latin ilia.

parole.significato: Subject to or pertaining to an illusion, often used in the sense of an unrealistic expectation or an unreachable goal o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin illūsīvus.

parole.significato: To put into a purse; to save, to store up.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin imbursāre, Late Latin imbursāre, from Latin im- (variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘in, inside’ usually affixed to verbs)) + bursa (“animal skin, oxhide; purse (usually made of leather or skin); supply of money, funds”) (from Ancient Greek βῠ́ρσᾰ (bŭ́rsă, “animal skin; skin stripped

parole.significato: The act of pawning or pledging; the state of being pawned.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin impignoratio: compare French impignoration.

parole.significato: Importance; significance.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin importantia.

parole.significato: Having relevant and crucial value; having import.
parole.testo: From Middle English important, from Medieval Latin important-, importāns. By surface analysis, import (“to be important”) + -ant. Displaced native Old English hēah and hefiġ.

parole.significato: To cause to become pregnant.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in 1540, the verb in 1605; borrowed from Medieval Latin impraegnātus, perfect passive participle of Latin impraegnō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of impregn; participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern Englis

parole.significato: To appropriate for private use.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin impropriātus, past participle of impropriāre (“to take as one's own, appropriate”), from Latin in- + proprius (“one's own”).

parole.significato: In the act of committing a misdeed.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Medieval Latin in flagrante delicto (literally “while the crime is blazing”), from in + flāgrō (“burn”) + dēlictō, form of dēlīctum (“crime, misdeed”).

parole.significato: Not intentional; not on purpose; not conscious.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin inadvertēns.

parole.significato: To lock away; to imprison, especially for breaking the law.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in 1528, the verb in 1575; borrowed from Medieval Latin incarcerātus, perfect passive participle of incarcerō (“to imprison”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from Latin in- (“in”) + carcer (“a prison”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of confining, or the state of being confined; imprisonment.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin incarcerātiō, equivalent to incarcerate + -ion.

parole.significato: Causing growth of new flesh i.e. healing or regenerative.
parole.testo: From Middle English incarnatif, incarnative, incarnatyf, incarnatyve, from Medieval Latin incarnātīvus.

parole.significato: To make into a castle.
parole.testo: First attested in 1552; borrowed from Medieval Latin incastellātus, perfect passive participle of incastellō (“to fortify, incastle, incastellate”) from in- (“in-: make into”) + castellum (“little fortification, castle; cistern”). Cognate with Italian incastellare.

parole.significato: To officially invest into a position of authority.
parole.testo: First attested in 1635; borrowed from Medieval Latin incathedrātus, perfect passive participle of incathedrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Synonym of censer (“religious ornamental container for burning incense”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin incēnsōrium. First attested in 1598. By surface analysis, incense + -ory.

parole.significato: Something that motivates, rouses, or encourages.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin incentīvus (“that strikes up or sets the tune”), from incinō (“to strike up”), from in- (“in, on”) + canō (“to sing”) + -ive. The formation appears to have been influenced by incendō (“to set on fire”).

parole.significato: Intelligently analytical and concise. (of a person or mental process)
parole.testo: Late Middle English (in the sense “cutting, penetrating”), borrowed from Medieval Latin incīsīvus, from incīdō (“to cut in, cut through”) + -īvus (“-ive”, adjectival suffix). Compare Middle French incisif.

parole.significato: That exists without having been created.
parole.testo: First attested in 1412, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English increat(e), borrowed from Medieval Latin increātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). See also in- (“not”), and create.

parole.significato: To accuse or bring criminal charges against.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin incrīminātus, perfect passive participle of Latin incrīminō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). First attested in 1736. By surface analysis, in- + criminate.

parole.significato: The act of incriminating someone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin incriminatus ( + -ion), from incrimino, from Latin crimino. Equivalent to incriminate + -ion.

parole.significato: The current holder of an office or title; (specifically, Christianity) the holder of an ecclesiastical benefice.
parole.testo: From Middle English incumbent, encumbent (“holder of an ecclesiastical benefice, dean, parson, etc.; cleric (?)”), from Medieval Latin incumbēns (“holder of a church position”) + Middle English -ent (suffix denoting one that causes, does, or promotes an action). Incumbēns is derived from Medieval La

parole.significato: A person considered alone, rather than as belonging to a group of people.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ From Medieval Latin indīviduālis, from Latin indīviduum (“an indivisible thing”), neuter of indīviduus (“indivisible, undivided”), from in + dīviduus (“divisible”), from dīvidō (“divide”). Displaced native Old English hād (“person, individual”).

parole.significato: A passive device that introduces inductance into an electrical circuit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin inductor, from Latin induco.

parole.significato: A person who, or an object or process that, is taken as being infallible.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin īnfallibilis, from Latin in- + fallibilis. Compare French infaillible. By surface analysis, in- + fallible.

parole.significato: Having a bad reputation; disreputable; notorious; unpleasant or evil; widely known, especially for something scornful.
parole.testo: From Middle English enfamouse, in-fames, infamous, from Medieval Latin īnfāmōsus, from Latin īnfāmis; by surface analysis, in- + famous. Displaced native Old English unhlīsful.

parole.significato: To surreptitiously penetrate, enter or gain access to.
parole.testo: From Middle English infiltrate (adjective), from Medieval Latin infiltrātus, from infiltrō.

parole.significato: The act or process of infiltrating, as of water into a porous substance, or of a fluid into the cells of an organ or pa…
parole.testo: From Middle English infiltracioun, from Medieval Latin infiltrātiōnem, infiltrātiō. By surface analysis, infiltrat(e) + -ion.

parole.significato: A place where sick or injured people are cared for, especially a small hospital; sickhouse.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin infirmaria, from Latin infirmus.

parole.significato: Of an inflating quality or tendency.
parole.testo: From Middle English inflātīve (“causing swelling; producing wind”), from Medieval Latin īnflātīvus, from īnflō (“to inflate; to blow into”). Compare the obsolete French adjective inflatif, inflative.

parole.significato: Having or exerting influence.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin īnfluentiālis, from īnfluentia + -ālis. By surface analysis, influence + -ial.

parole.significato: Providing or communicating information.
parole.testo: From Middle English informatory, from Medieval Latin īnfōrmātōrius. By surface analysis, inform + -atory.

parole.significato: To make furious or mad with anger; to fill with fury.
parole.testo: First attested in 1667; borrowed from Medieval Latin infuriātus (“enraged”), perfect passive participle of infuriō (“to enrage”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin furia (“rage, fury, frenzy”); perhaps via Italian infuriato.

parole.significato: incapable of being generated or created.
parole.testo: From Middle English ingenerable, from Medieval Latin ingenerābilis.

parole.significato: A lack of security; uncertainty.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin īnsēcūritās. By surface analysis, insecure + -ity.

parole.significato: The condition of being insipid; insipidness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin īnsipiditās. By surface analysis, insipid + -ity.

parole.significato: immediately; instantly; without delay.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Medieval Latin īnstanter (“immediately”), originally “vehemently” in Classical Latin.

parole.significato: The production of an instance, example, or specific application of a general classification, principle, theory, etc.
parole.testo: A coinage of the twentieth century, from instantiate + -ion, itself coined in 1946 from instance + -ate. parole.significato: Essential or central; of great importance or relevance.
parole.testo: From Middle English instrumental, instrumentale, from Medieval Latin īnstrūmentālis, equivalent to instrument + -al.

parole.significato: Understanding; careful consideration, attention.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin intendimentum.

parole.significato: Intended or planned; done deliberately or voluntarily.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin intentiōnālis, from intentiō + -ālis. By surface analysis, intention + -al.

parole.significato: The situation or occurrence in which two or more things act upon one another to produce an effect; the effect resulting…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin interāctiō.

parole.significato: A person who takes part in dialogue or conversation: a locutive partner.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin interlocūtor, from the agent noun counterpart (via the suffix -tor) of Latin interloquor (“speak between, issue an interlocutory decree”), from inter- + loquor (“speak”).

parole.significato: Being between two extremes, or in the middle of a range.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin intermediātus, perfect passive participle of intermediō (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), further from intermedius (“intermediate”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To mediate, to be an intermediate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin intermediātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

parole.significato: To make timid or afraid; to cause to feel fear or nervousness; to deter, especially by threats of violence.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin intimidātus, perfect passive participle of Latin intimidō (“to intimidate, terrify”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + timidus (“afraid, timid”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); see timid.

parole.significato: To intone or recite (words), especially emphatically or in a chanting manner.
parole.testo: First attested in 1795; borrowed from Medieval Latin intonātus, perfect passive participle of intonō (“to vocalize, chant”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (inchoative prefix) + tonus (“pitch, tone”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); doublet of intone. Cognate with French entonner, Italian into

parole.significato: The state of being allowed to enter; admittance
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin intrōmissiō, intrōmissiōn- (“introduction, admission; usurpation”), intro- (“into”) + missiō (“sending”), from Latin intrōmissus (“sent in, introduced, let in, admitted”), perfect passive participle of intrōmittō (“send in, let in”).

parole.significato: sheathed
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin invāgīnātus, past participle of Medieval Latin invāgīnāre, from in- + vāgīna (“sheath”).

parole.significato: The stock of an item on hand at a particular location or business.
parole.testo: From Middle English inventorie, from Medieval Latin inventōrium, alteration of Late Latin inventārium, from Latin inveniō (“to find out”).

parole.significato: Made brilliant or bright; irradiated, illuminated.
parole.testo: From Middle English irradiate (“illuminated, shining”), borrowed from Medieval Latin irradiātus, perfect passive participle of irradiō, from ir- (“against; into; on, upon”) + radiō (“to cause to radiate, irradiate; to emit beams, radiate”), from radius (“ray of light; rod, staff; spoke of a wheel”)

parole.significato: I don't understand any of it; it makes no sense.
parole.testo: First quoted as it was Greek to me in Julius Caesar by Shakespeare, possibly translated from a sentence in Medieval Latin.

parole.significato: Pertaining to Italy.
parole.testo: From Middle English Italian, from Medieval Latin Italiānus, from Latin Italia (“Italy”). By surface analysis, Italia + -n.

parole.significato: A travelling around.
parole.testo: From itinerate + -ion, ultimately borrowed from Medieval Latin itinerātiō, from itineror (“travel”), from itiner-.

parole.significato: Bragging or boasting, especially in a false manner to another's detriment.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin jactitio, from iactitō (“throw, fling; boast, brag; utter, mention”).

parole.significato: The sweet and edible drupes (fruits) of several Mediterranean and African species of small trees.
parole.testo: From Middle English jujube, from Medieval Latin jujuba or Old French jujube, perhaps via Old Occitan from Classical Latin zīzyphum, zīzyphus, from Ancient Greek ζίζυφον (zízuphon)․ First attested in the 14th century.

parole.significato: To attend a junket; to feast.
parole.testo: From Middle English jonket (“basket made of rushes”), from Medieval Latin iuncta, possibly from Latin iuncus (“rush, reed”) and therefore a possible doublet of jonquil. parole.significato: A sworn statement concerning where, when, and before whom an oath has been made.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin iūrātus (“sworn [man]”) or iūrātum (“[that which is] sworn”), from Latin iūrō (“to swear an oath”). As a medieval office, via French jurat, via Occitan juré.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the lips or labia.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Medieval Latin labiālis (“of or pertaining to the lips”), from labium (“a lip”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). By surface analysis, labi(um) + -al.

parole.significato: A laboratory.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin labōrātōrium. Doublet of laboratory.

parole.significato: A room, building or institution equipped for scientific research, experimentation or analysis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin labōrātōrium.

parole.significato: A place where stone monuments and fragments of archaeological interest are exhibited.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin lapidārium, from Latin lapidārius (“stony; stone (relational)”).

parole.significato: Synonym of calamine, a pink form of zinc oxide formed as a byproduct during sublimation.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin lapis calamīnāris, from lapis (“stone, mineral”) + calamīnāris (“of or related to calamine”), from calamīna (“calamine”) + -āris (“-ary: forming adjectives”), from Latin cadmia, from Ancient Greek κᾰδμῐ́ᾱ (kădmĭ́ā), variant of Κᾰδμείᾱ (Kădmeíā), from Κάδμος (Kádmos, “Cadmus”) + -

parole.significato: A deep blue stone, used in making jewelry, and traditionally used to make the pigment ultramarine.
parole.testo: From Middle English lapis lazuli, from Medieval Latin lapis (“stone”) + lazulī, genitive singular of lazulum (“lapis lazuli, azure, the sky”), from Arabic لَازُوَرْد (lāzuward, “lapis lazuli, azure”), from Persian لاجورد (lâjvard). Compare azure, of the same origin.

parole.significato: A mineral of metamorphosed limestones. Lazurite forms the gemstone lapis lazuli, and crushed lazurite provided the ultr…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin lazur (“lapis lazuli”) (from Arabic لَازَوَرْد (lāzaward), from Persian لاژورد (lâžvard)) + -ite.

parole.significato: A spoken lesson or exposition, usually delivered to a group.
parole.testo: From Middle English lecture, lectour, letture, letteur, lettur, lectury, from Medieval Latin or Late Latin lectura (“reading”), from Latin lectus, past participle of legō (“to read, recite”). Doublet of lector.

parole.significato: A literary collection of legends, particularly those detailing the life of a saint.
parole.testo: Neuter form of Medieval Latin legendarius, from Latin legendus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a legend or to legends.
parole.testo: From legend + -ary; from Medieval Latin legendārius. Earlier it was a noun meaning "a collection of legends" (1510s) (Medieval Latin legendārium, Old French legendier), from Latin legenda. In English, both the noun and the adjective first appeared in the 16th century.

parole.significato: In accordance with the law or established legal forms and requirements.
parole.testo: From Middle English legitimat, legytymat, from Medieval Latin lēgitimātus, perfect passive participle of Latin lēgitimō (“to make legal”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from Latin lēgitimus (“lawful”), originally "fixed by law, in line with the law," from Latin lēx (“law”). Originally "lawfu

parole.significato: Of the Leguminosae family of peas, beans etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English leguminous, from Medieval Latin legūminōsus, ultimately from oblique stem of Latin legūmen, legūminis (“bean, pulse”) + -ous.

parole.significato: An object, usually made of glass, that focuses or defocuses the light that passes through it.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lēns (“lentil”), with Medieval Latin later taking on the sense of “lens”, a semantic loan from Arabic عَدَسَة (ʕadasa, “lentil; optic lens”); the similar shape is the common factor.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a lens.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English lenticular, lenticuler, borrowed from Medieval Latin lenticulāris (“lentil-shaped”), from Latin lenticula, from lēns + -cula, ultimately from Latin lēns (“lentil”).

parole.significato: a cloud species which consists of rounded lens shaped of cloud, often forming near mountains. Associated with cirrocumu…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin lenticulāris (“lentil-shaped”), from Latin lenticula, from lēns + -cula, ultimately from Latin lēns (“lentil”).

parole.significato: A 13th-century coin minted in Europe and used in England as a debased form of the sterling silver penny; it was outlawe…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin leōnīna + English -ine (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’). Leōnīna is a feminine singular form of Latin leōnīnus (see etymology 1), and may refer to the use of a lion motif on the coin: see the 1787 quotation.

parole.significato: Synonym of leprosarium.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin leprōsāria, from leprōsus (“leprous”) + -āria, now usually under the influence of Spanish leprosería.

parole.significato: An isolated building or community used to house lepers, usually in permanent quarantine from the rest of society.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin leprōsārium, from leprōsus (“leprous”) + -ārium (“-ary: building related to”). Doublet of leprosery.

parole.significato: A state of extreme torpor, sopor or apathy, especially with lack of emotion, energy or enthusiasm; (loosely) sluggishne…
parole.testo: From Middle English litargie, from Medieval Latin litargia, from Late Latin lēthārgia, borrowed from Ancient Greek ληθᾱργῐ́ᾱ (lēthārgĭ́ā, “drowsiness”), from λήθᾱργος (lḗthārgos, “forgetful, lethargic”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: A Frankish vassal or tenant in the Early Middle Ages.
parole.testo: 1750, from Medieval Latin leudēs pl (“vassals or followers of the king”), from Frankish *liudi (“people”), from Proto-Germanic *liudiz (“people”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁léwdʰis (“man, people”). parole.significato: A piece of land having a value of one pound per year.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin lībrāta, from Latin lībra (“pound”).

parole.significato: Any of various gastropods with a conical shell shape (patelliform) and a strong, muscular foot that they use to create…
parole.testo: From Middle English lempet, from Old English lempedu (“lamprey”), borrowed from Medieval Latin lampreda, alteration of Late Latin lampetra (“lamprey”), whose further origin is unknown, though is traditionally thought to derive from lambō (“to lick, lap”) + petra (“stone, rock”). parole.significato: To mark with lines.
parole.testo: First attested in 1558; borrowed from Medieval Latin līneātus, perfect passive participle of līneō (“to draw a line; (classically) to reduce to a straight line, make straight”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from līnea (“a line”).

parole.significato: A torch, used to light dark streets.
parole.testo: Plausibly a modification of Medieval Latin linchinus (“candle”), an alteration of Latin lynchinus, itself from Ancient Greek λύχνος (lúkhnos, “lamp”).

parole.significato: The state or condition of being livid (dark or pallid).
parole.testo: From livid + -ness, originally after Medieval Latin līviditās.

parole.significato: To separate (a substance) into soluble and insoluble components through percolation; to leach.
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Medieval Latin lixīvio, lixīviātus, or formed from the root of lixīvium, lixīvia, from lixīvius (“made into lye”), from lixa (“water, lye, ashes”).

parole.significato: An entryway or reception area; vestibule; passageway; corridor.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin lobia, lobium, laubia (“a portico, covered way, gallery”), borrowed from Frankish *laubijā (“arbour, shelter”), related to Old English lēaf (“foliage”).
