parole.significato: A professional person (such as a doctor or clergyman) who temporarily fulfills the duties of another.
parole.testo: Existing in English since the seventeenth century: from Medieval Latin locum tenēns (literally “one holding a place”). Doublet of lieutenant.

parole.significato: Any of various state officials or functionaries in the Byzantine Empire.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin logotheta, borrowed from Byzantine Greek λογοθέτης (logothétēs), from Ancient Greek λόγος (lógos) + θέτης (thétēs).

parole.significato: A medicine in a soft form taken by licking; a lambative, a linctus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin lohoc, looch, from Arabic لَعْق (laʕq, “to lick”).

parole.significato: Relating to any person called Lothar or Lothair.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Lōthariānus, from Lōtharius + -iānus. By surface analysis, Lothar + -ian.

parole.significato: Relating to any person called Louis or Ludwig.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Lūdovīciānus, from Lūdovīcus + -iānus. By surface analysis, Ludovic + -ian.

parole.significato: A month of an average of approximately 29.53 days, measured from a lunar phase until the return of that same phase.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin lūnātiō.

parole.significato: One who plays the lute, a lutist.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin lutanista, from lutana (“lute”), from Middle French lut. By surface analysis, lute + -n- + -ist.

parole.significato: To furnish with machicolations.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin machicolātus, perfect participle of machicolāre, from Old French machicoller, from machicolleis (“machicolation”), from Old Occitan machacol, from macar (“to crush”) + col (“neck”).

parole.significato: Leanness; emaciation.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin macilentia, from macilentus (“lean, thin”).

parole.significato: A landmark document that sets out rights or important principles.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English Magna Carta, borrowed from Medieval Latin Magna Carta, from Latin magna (“great”) + carta (“charter”).

parole.significato: majestic
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin maiestāticus.

parole.significato: Increase; enlargement.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin maiōrātiō, from maiōrō (“to augment”), from Latin maior. By surface analysis, majorate + -ion. Compare French majoration.

parole.significato: To beat into shape with a hammer.
parole.testo: First attested in 1598; borrowed from Medieval Latin malleātus, perfect passive participle of malleō (“to beat with a hammer”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Things do not always work out as they are planned.
parole.testo: Calque of Medieval Latin homo proponit, sed Deus disponit, coined in Thomas à Kempis's De Imitatione Christi.

parole.significato: Any of various plants of the genus Mandragora.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mandragora, from Latin mandragorās.

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Mandragora, certain of which are said to have medicinal or aphrodisiac properties; the root of t…
parole.testo: From Middle English mandrake, mandroke, an alteration of mandragora with the ending -dragora reinterpreted as related to dragon and replaced with native drake, from Old English mandragora, from Medieval Latin mandragorās, from Ancient Greek μανδραγόρας (mandragóras).

parole.significato: A house inhabited by the minister of a parish.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mānsus (“dwelling”), from Latin manēre (“to remain”), whence also manor, mansion. Doublet of mas.

parole.significato: Handwritten, or by extension manually typewritten, as opposed to being mechanically reproduced.
parole.testo: 1597, from Medieval Latin manūscrīptus, a calque of Germanic origin, equivalent to Latin manū (ablative of manus (“hand”)) + Latin scrīptus (past participle of scribere (“to write”)). Not found in Classical Latin.

parole.significato: A book, composition or any other document, written by hand (or manually typewritten), not mechanically reproduced.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin manūscrīptum (“writing by hand”), a calque of Germanic origin: compare Middle Low German hantschrift (“manuscript, document”), Middle Dutch hantscrift (“manuscript”) (c. 1451), Old High German hantgiskrīb (“handwriting, document, manuscript”), Middle High German hantschrift, hant

parole.significato: The wife of a marquess.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin marchionissa, feminine form of marchion, from Late Latin marca, from Frankish *markōn (“to mark, mark out, to press with the foot”), from Proto-Germanic *markō (“area, region, edge, rim, border”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or located at or near a margin or edge; also figurative usages of location and margin (edge).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin marginālis, equivalent to margin + -al.

parole.significato: The right of the lord of the fee to dispose of the heiress, later also of the male heir, in marriage.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin marītāgium. Doublet of marriage.

parole.significato: Synonym of maritage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin marītāgium.

parole.significato: A lozenge-shaped piece of metal, used in making scale mail.
parole.testo: From Middle English maskel, maskle, maskle, from Medieval Latin mascula, from Germanic source. Cognate with Medieval Latin macula and Old French macle, macule. Compare English mesh). Doublet of mail.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to mathematics.
parole.testo: From Middle English mathematicalle, mathematical, from Medieval Latin mathēmaticālis.

parole.significato: In the Merovingian kingdoms, the king’s steward and, by the 7th century, de facto regent.
parole.testo: Calque of Medieval Latin maior palātiī.

parole.significato: A calendar of the days of the month or of all the days of the year divided by month, particularly as a table of informa…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mēnologium, from Ancient and Byzantine Greek μηνολόγιον (mēnológion), from μήν (mḗn, “month”) + λόγιον (lógion, “writing, record, announcement”), itself from λόγος (lógos, “writing, recording”). Doublet of menologion, menologe, and menology.

parole.significato: The study of months; the names and system of months within a given calendar.
parole.testo: Partially from meno- (“month-”) + -ology (“study, account”) and partially from anglicization of Medieval Latin mēnologium and Byzantine Greek μηνολόγιον (mēnológion), q.v. Doublet of menologion, menologium, and menologe.

parole.significato: measurable
parole.testo: From Middle English mensurable, from Medieval Latin mensūrābilis. Doublet of measurable. See also -able.

parole.significato: A descendant of Merovech; a Merovingian.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Merovingus, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *Mārīwīg [a male given name composed of *mārī (“famous”) + *wīg (“fight”)] + *-ing. By surface analysis, Merovech + -ing. Cognate with Old English Merewīoingas (a hapax legomenon in the genitive case).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to metaphysics.
parole.testo: From Middle English metaphisicalle, methafisical, from Medieval Latin metaphysicālis. By surface analysis, meta- + physical.

parole.significato: An ornamental shrub, Daphne mezereum, having purple flowers and bright red fruit.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mezereon, mezereum, from Arabic مَازَرْيُون (māzaryūn).

parole.significato: A mining business.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mineria, minaria, from Old French miniere.

parole.significato: Synonym of Poor Clare: a nun of the Order of Saint Clare.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin minorissa, from Latin minor (“little, lesser”) + -issa (“-ess”), under influence from Norman frere-menouresse and Middle French sereur meneuresse (“lesser sister”), from menour (“minor”) + -esse (“-ess”), after the model of Medieval Latin Fratres Minores (“Lesser Brothers”), chos

parole.significato: Synonym of Franciscan: a friar of the Order of Friars Minor.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Minorita, from Latin minor + -īta (“-ite”), from Ordo Fratres Minores (“Order of Friars Minor”), literally the "Order of the Lesser Brothers", chosen by St. Francis to inculcate humility in its members. Equivalent to minor + -ite. Doublet of minister.

parole.significato: The abdominal wall.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mirac, mirach, from Arabic مَرَقّ (maraqq, “delicate and sensible part of the venter”), from رَقَّ (raqqa, “to be soft”).

parole.significato: A written message; a letter, note or memo.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin missīvus, from mittō (“to send”).

parole.significato: A member of a Christian sect which held that Jesus Christ has one nature, as opposed to the Chalcedonian view that Chri…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin monophysita, from Byzantine Greek μονοφυσίτης (monophusítēs), from Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos, “single”) + φύσις (phúsis, “nature”).

parole.significato: A requiem mass or other commemoration of a deceased person held one month after burial.
parole.testo: From Middle English monethes mynde under influence from Medieval Latin dies mensis (“day of the month”) and Old English ġemynd, whose principal sense was "memory".

parole.significato: measles, rubeola
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin morbillus, from Latin morbus (“disease”) + -illus (“diminutive suffix”).

parole.significato: Resembling the erythematous, maculopapular rash of measles.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin morbillus (“measles”) + -form. See morbilli for more.

parole.significato: Synonym of morello (“type of cherry”).
parole.testo: From Middle English morel, morell, from Anglo-Norman and Old French morel, morele, morelle and their etymon Medieval Latin maurella, morella, from Late Latin maurus, morus (“black”) + Latin -ella (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: Servile acquiescence; unqualified sycophancy towards a bully or a tyrant.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mōrigerātiō. Compare Middle English morigeracioun (“character or nature”).

parole.significato: The act of lingering with pleasure on an impure thought.
parole.testo: Calque of Medieval Latin dēlectātiō mōrōsa, used by Thomas Aquinas in the Summa Theologiae.

parole.significato: A blemish or mark on the skin, especially a blister caused by scurvy.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin morphea, perhaps from Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “form, shape”). Doublet of morphea.

parole.significato: Of one’s own free will, of one’s own volition.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin motu proprio, from ablative form of classical Latin motus (“motion”) + proprius (“one’s own”).

parole.significato: A secret killing, distinguished from simple homicide in that the victim and the killer are unknown.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Medieval Latin murdrum, a Germanic borrowing from Frankish *murþr, *morþr, from Proto-Germanic *murþrą (“murder”). More at murder.

parole.significato: An act or instance of murmuring.
parole.testo: 1350–1400; Medieval Latin murmuratio (“murmuring, grumbling”), equivalent to murmur + -ation. The “flock of starlings” sense is probably derived from the sound of the very large groups that starlings form at dusk.

parole.significato: The use of chromatically altered tones in the contrapuntal music of the 10th to the 16th centuries.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mūsica ficta (literally “fashioned music”).

parole.significato: The point of the celestial sphere, directly opposite the zenith; inferior pole of the horizon; point of the celestial s…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin nadir, from Arabic نَظِير السَّمْت (naẓīr as-samt), composed of نَظِير (naẓīr, “counterpart, corresponding to”) and السَّمْت (as-samt, “the zenith”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the nose or to the nasion.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Medieval Latin nāsālis, from nāsus (“the nose”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). Doublet of nasalis.

parole.significato: To make necessary; to behove; to require (something) to be brought about.
parole.testo: From earlier necessitat, from Medieval Latin necessitātus, perfect past participle of necessitō (“to make necessary”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix, of participial origin)), from Classical Latin necessitās (“necessity, need”) + -ō. Necessitās is derived from necesse (“unavoidable”) (from ne- (“not”

parole.significato: Negative; negating.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin negātōrius (possibly via Middle French negatoire), from Latin negātus.

parole.significato: A water lily, especially the European white water lily (Nymphaea alba) or the yellow water lily (Nuphar lutea).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin nenuphar, from Arabic نِلُوفَر (nilūfar), نِينُوفَر (nīnūfar), from Middle Persian nylw(k)pl (nīlōpal, “lotus, water-lily”), from Sanskrit नीलोत्पल (nīlotpala, “blue lotus”), from नील (nīla, “blue”) + उत्पल (utpala, “lotus, water-lily”). Compare French nénufar.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or affected with nephritis or nephritic syndrome.
parole.testo: From Middle English neufretic, from Medieval Latin nefreticus; compare Classical Latin nephrīticus; equivalent to nephritis + -ic = nephr- (“kidney”) + itis (“inflammation”) + -ic (“related”).

parole.significato: Early Modern English spelling of nerve
parole.testo: Recorded since circa [1374] as Middle English nerve, from Medieval Latin nervus (“nerve”), from Latin nervus (“sinew”). Doublet of neuron and sinew.

parole.significato: A bundle of neurons with their connective tissue sheaths, blood vessels and lymphatics.
parole.testo: Recorded since circa 1374 as Middle English nerve, from Medieval Latin nervus (“nerve”), from Latin nervus (“sinew”). Doublet of neuron and sinew. Verb sense 4 (“to get on (someone’s) nerves”) is chiefly a semantic loan from German nerven.

parole.significato: Nihil
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin nichil, from nihil.

parole.significato: Of, from, or pertaining to Nicosia, the capital of Cyprus and Northern Cyprus.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Nicosianus, from Nicosia + -ānus. Equivalent to Nicosia + -an.

parole.significato: Emitting a strong, unpleasant odor, especially one like that of cooking fat or similar greasy substances.
parole.testo: From nidor (“the unpleasant smell of some cooked animal substances”) + -ous, or from Medieval Latin nidorosus.

parole.significato: Synonym of zinc oxide, particularly white forms.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin nihil album (“white nothing”), from late medieval confusion of German nichts (“nothing”) and nix with Latin nix (“snow, snow-white thing”), used for white forms of zinc oxide. Doublet of nill.

parole.significato: Synonym of zinc oxide, particularly white forms used in medicine and cosmetics.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin nil and nihil (“nothing”) to represent German nichts and nix (“nothing”), confused with Latin nix (“snow, snow-white thing”), used for white forms of zinc oxide. Doublet of nihil album.

parole.significato: The night office of the Christian liturgy of the Hours, such as is performed in monasteries.
parole.testo: From Middle English nocturne, borrowed from Medieval Latin nocturna, noun use of the feminine form of Latin nocturnus (“nocturnal, of the night”), derived from nox (“night”).

parole.significato: The state of being unwilling; nolition.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin nolleitās, from nolle (“to be unwilling”) + -ity. Formed on the model of velleity.

parole.significato: Senses with an unfavourable connotation.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English notoryous, from Medieval Latin nōtōrius (“evident, known; famous, well-known; infamous”), from Latin nōtus (“known, recognized; familiar, widely known; famous, well-known; infamous”) + -tōrius (suffix forming adjectives). parole.significato: Of or related to Nubia, its animals, or the Nubian people.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Nubianus directly and via French nubien, from Nubia + -anus (“-an: forming adjectives”), from Nubae (“ancient Nubians”) + -ia (“-ia: forming place names”), from Koine Greek Νοῦβαι (Noûbai), q.v. Equivalent to Nubia + -an or Nuba + -ian.

parole.significato: The spinal cord.
parole.testo: From Middle English nucha, nuche, nuca, nuka, nuke (“spinal cord”), borrowed from Medieval Latin nucha (“spinal cord; nape of the neck”). Doublet of nuque.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the back or nape of the neck.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin nuchālis, from nucha + -ālis, from Arabic نُخَاع (nuḵāʕ, “spinal cord”).

parole.significato: A child of unknown parentage; an orphan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin nullius filius (“nobody's son”), from Latin nullius + filius.

parole.significato: An evergreen tree (Myristica fragrans) cultivated in the East Indies for its spicy seeds.
parole.testo: From Middle English notemege, notemuge, a partial translation of Medieval Latin nux muga, a variant of Medieval Latin nux muscata (“musky nut”). Compare also Old French nois mugede. For the term used in various ball sports, see Wikipedia.

parole.significato: A form of the letter o modified by the addition of a diacritical “tail”: ⟨ǫ⟩, used in Old Norse.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin o caudāta (literally “tailed o”).

parole.significato: The holder of a monastic rank or office below that of superior.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin obedientiarius, from Latin oboedientia (“obedience”) + la + -arius. By surface analysis, from obedient + -i- (“connecting vowel”) + -ary.

parole.significato: A brief notice of a person's death, especially one published in a newspaper or other publication; also (obsolete), the…
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₁epi Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin obituārius (“obituary”) + English -ary (suffix denoting something relating to another thing or used in a place). parole.significato: To cloud or obscure (something).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin obnebulatus, perfect passive participle of obnebulare (“to overcloud”), from ob- + nebula + -are. Compare obnubilate, derived from the unrelated Latin nūbēs.

parole.significato: The characteristic of being obstinate.
parole.testo: From Middle English obstinance, obstinaunce, from Medieval Latin obstināntia, equivalent to obstinant + -ance.

parole.significato: The act of obviating; deterrence or prevention.
parole.testo: From Middle English obviacioun, from Medieval Latin obviātiō.

parole.significato: Occurring or appearing irregularly from time to time, but not often; incidental.
parole.testo: From Middle English occasyonal, from Medieval Latin occāsiōnālis and Old French ocasionel. By surface analysis, occasion + -al.

parole.significato: To occasion.
parole.testo: From Middle English occasionaten, from Medieval Latin occāsiōnātus, perfect passive participle of occāsiō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, occasion + -ate.

parole.significato: Having a distinctive odor.
parole.testo: From Middle English odorous, from Medieval Latin odōrōsus, equivalent to odor + -ous.

parole.significato: A person who officiates at a religious ceremony (in Christianity, at any ceremony other than the Eucharist).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin officiāns, present participle of officiō, officiāre (“to perform a duty or service”) (not to be confused with Classical officiō, officere (“to obstruct, hinder”)), a denominal verb from officium (“duty, service”).

parole.significato: A gum resin from trees of the genus Boswellia, formerly used as a medicine and now mainly as incense.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin olibanum, from Latin oleum libani, the first word meaning oil and the second from Ancient Greek λίβανος (líbanos, “frankincense (Boswellia sacra)”), from a Semitic source, compare Proto-Semitic *laban- (“white”). parole.significato: Being everywhere simultaneously.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin omnipraesēns, equivalent to omni- + present.

parole.significato: The capacity to know everything.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin omniscientia (“all-knowledge”), from Latin omni- (“all”), and scient from the Latin scientia (“knowledge”).

parole.significato: Having total knowledge.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin omnisciens (“all-knowing”), from Latin omnis (“all”) + sciens (“knowing”) (further analysable via scient).

parole.significato: effective; practical; operative
parole.testo: Originally from Medieval Latin operātōrium, from a participle of Late Latin operor. The modern senses may be derived independently of the obsolete senses.

parole.significato: Synonym of ophthalmitis (“inflammation of the eye”).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin obtalmia and Old French obtalmie, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀφθαλμός (ophthalmós). Re-classicized from the Greek spelling, instead of archaic obtalmy (“eye inflammation, (also?) longsightedness”).

parole.significato: Relating to, resembling, or containing opium.
parole.testo: From Middle English opiate, from Medieval Latin opiātus.

parole.significato: The physics of light and vision: basic optical science.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin opticus (“optic, optical”), from Ancient Greek ὀπτικός (optikós), equivalent to optic + -ics.

parole.significato: The spiritual effect in the performance of a religious rite that is ascribed chiefly or exclusively to the disposition…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin opus operantis (literally “work of the worker”).

parole.significato: The spiritual effect in the performance of a religious rite which accrues from the virtue inherent in it, or by grace i…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin opus operātum (literally “work done”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to, or forming an orbit (such as the orbit of a moon, planet, or spacecraft).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin orbitālis, from orbita (“a track or rut; a circuit, orbit”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix), equivalent to orbit + -al. Doublet of orbitalis.

parole.testo: From Middle English ordel, ordal, from Medieval Latin ordālium or inherited from its source Old English ordēl, ordāl (“ordeal, judgement”), from Proto-West Germanic *uʀdailī (“judgement”, literally “an out-dealing”), from *uʀdailijan (“to deal out; dispense”). parole.significato: To cause (someone or something) to be; to bring (someone or something) into existence; to produce or initiate a person…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin orīginātus, perfect passive participle of orīginō (“to begin, give rise to”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more), from orīgō (orīgin- in compounds) + -ō. Compare Italian originare and Spanish originar. By surface analysis, origin + -ate.

parole.significato: Founded on, having its origin in (something).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin orīginātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more. By surface analysis, origin + -ate.

parole.significato: The origin story of a tribe or people.
parole.testo: Derived from Medieval Latin origo gentis (“origin, beginning of a people”).

parole.significato: A fern of the genus Osmunda, especially the royal fern, Osmunda regalis.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin osmunda (“royal fern”). Compare osmund.

parole.significato: To exhibit in show; to represent; to mimic.
parole.testo: Late 14th c. as Middle English pagent, from Medieval Latin pagina (“play in a cycle of mystery plays”), perhaps from Latin pāgina (“page of a book”).

parole.significato: To number the pages of (a book or other document); to foliate.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin paginare, from Latin pagina.

parole.significato: Paludinal: characteristic of or relating to marsh, swamp or fen.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin palūdīnōsus (“marshy, swampy”), ultimately from palūs. Sense 2 from translingual Paludina + -ous.

parole.significato: The purulent inflammation of a digit.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin panāritium.

parole.significato: The office of a pope.
parole.testo: Circa 14th century, from Middle English papacie, papassie, from Medieval Latin pāpātia, from Latin pāpa (“pope”) + -tia (“office, rank”) (English -cy).

parole.significato: A flourish made after or below one's signature, originally to prevent forgery.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English paraf, from Medieval Latin paraffus or its etymon Middle French paraphe, paraffe, shortening of paragraphe, from Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a woman's parapherna
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin paraphernālis, from Late Latin parapherna + Latin -ālis (suffix forming adjectives). By surface analysis, paraphern(a) + -al.

parole.significato: Miscellaneous items, especially the set of equipment required for a particular activity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin paraphernālia (“goods which a wife brings over and above her dowry”), use as noun (short for paraphernālia bona (“paraphernal goods”)) of neuter plural of paraphernālis, from Late Latin parapherna + Latin -ālis (suffix forming adjectives), from Ancient Greek παράφερνα (p

parole.significato: Using, containing, or within parenthesis.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin parentheticus (from Late Latin parenthesis or Ancient Greek παρένθετος (parénthetos), + -icus) + -al. By surface analysis, par- + en- + thetical.

parole.significato: The unique human position in Spinozan philosophy, where humans are simultaneously (i) 'finite modalities' as 'contingen…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin partiālitās. Doublet of partiality. Used by the British philosopher Harold Foster Hallett in his book Aeternitas: A Spinozistic Study (1930).

parole.significato: That divides something into parts.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English partitif, borrowed from Medieval Latin partītīvus, from Latin partītus + -īvus.

parole.significato: A book in which the sufferings of saints and martyrs are described
parole.testo: From Middle English passyonarye, from Medieval Latin passiōnārium, from Late Latin passiō, passiōn- (“suffering, enduring; passion”) + Latin -ārium (“-ary”).

parole.significato: Given to strong feeling, sometimes romantic, sexual, or both.
parole.testo: From Middle English passionat, from Medieval Latin passiōnātus (“affected, impassioned, libidinous, easely angered”). Equivalent to passion + -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Compare French passionné.

parole.significato: The rank of a patrician
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin patriciātus. By surface analysis, patrician + -ate.

parole.significato: The study of the works of the early Christian Church Fathers.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin patristica, from Latin pater (“father”).

parole.significato: Liable to sin; subject to transgress the divine law.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin peccābilis, from Latin peccō (“to sin”).

parole.significato: Sinful.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin peccaminōsus, from peccāmen (“sin”), from peccō (“to sin”).

parole.significato: The bathing of the feet.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pediluvium.

parole.significato: pejoration; process of making or becoming worse
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin peiōritās.

parole.significato: An appendage; something attached to something else.
parole.testo: From Middle English, probably from Medieval Latin pendiculum (“appendage”), from Late Latin pendiculus (“cord, noose”), from Latin pendere (“to weigh”).

parole.significato: That can or does physically penetrate something; piercing, penetrating.
parole.testo: From Middle English penetratyve, penetratif, from Medieval Latin penetrativus, from (the participle stem of) Latin penetrāre (“to penetrate”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to penance or penitence.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin paenitentiālis, from Latin paenitentia (“repentance”). Attested since the 16th century.

parole.significato: A state or federal prison for convicted felons; (loosely) a prison.
parole.testo: From Middle English penitentiary, from Medieval Latin pēnitentiārius (“place of penitence”), from Latin paenitentia (“penitence”), term used by the Quakers in Pennsylvania during the 1790s, describing a place for penitents to dwell upon their sins.

parole.significato: Miserly; excessively cheap.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pēnūriōsus. See penury from Latin penuria (“want”), related to paene (“scarcely”), c. 1400. Compare French pénurie.

parole.significato: A thorough rubbing, as with an ointment or embrocation.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin perfricātiō, from perfricō.

parole.significato: Any monetary or other incidental benefit beyond salary.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin perquīsītum (“something acquired for profit”).

parole.significato: A weapon used to hurl stones
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin petraria, from Latin petra (“stone”).

parole.significato: A flammable liquid ranging in color from clear to very dark brown and black, consisting mainly of hydrocarbons, occurri…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin petroleum. Doublet of petrol.

parole.significato: Any of various compounds of transition metals or of rare earths that exhibit phosphorescence.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin phosphorus.

parole.significato: The innermost of the meninges, the membranes that surround the brain and spinal cord.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pia māter (literally “tender mother”).

parole.significato: A size of type between small pica and English, now standardized as 12-point.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pica (“pica: a service book”), possibly from Latin pīca (“magpie”) after the piebald appearance of the typeset page (cf. pie (“disordered type”)). parole.significato: The powder of aloes with canella, formerly officinal, employed as a cathartic.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin picra, from Ancient Greek πίκρα (píkra, “a kind of antidote”), from πικρός (pikrós, “sharp, bitter”).

parole.significato: Synonym of pignoratitious.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pignoratus, variant of earlier Latin pignerātus (“pledged, guaranteed”).

parole.significato: to pledge or pawn
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pignoro, variant of earlier Latin pignerō (“to pledge, to guarantee”).

parole.significato: A person invested with full powers, especially as the diplomatic agent of a sovereign state, (originally) charged with…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin plēnipotentiārius (“having full power”), Late Latin plēnipotēns, from plēnus (“full”) + potēns (“mighty, powerful”).

parole.significato: Each of a pair of smooth serous membranes which line the thorax and envelop the lungs in humans and other mammals.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Medieval Latin pleura.

parole.significato: A fold or crease, especially of skin or other tissue.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin, from Latin plicare (“to fold”).

parole.significato: Synonym of polysemic.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin polysēmus, from Ancient Greek πολύσημος (polúsēmos), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + σημαίνω (sēmaínō, “I signify, mean”).

parole.significato: The use of many conjunctions to achieve an overwhelming effect in a sentence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin polysyndeton, itself from Byzantine Greek πολυσύνδετον (polusúndeton, literally “many connected”).

parole.significato: The pulp or pulplike matter remaining from a substance pressed to extract its juice or oil.
parole.testo: [Alt: Red grape flesh and seeds] From Late Middle English pomis, pomys (“cider; pulp of plants pressed to extract their juice or oil”), probably from Medieval Latin pōmācium, pōmātium (“cider”), possibly a variant of pomaceum (although first attested later), from Latin pōmum (“fruit; fruit tree”) (u

parole.significato: Synonym of ointment, particularly thick waxy ointments scented with fruit used to beautify the skin or hair.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pomatum (“cider, ointment”), from Latin pōmum (“fruit, apple”) + -ātum (“-ate: forming nouns”). Doublet of pomate, pomade, and pomace.

parole.significato: To preside as a bishop, especially at mass.
parole.testo: From the past participle stem of Medieval Latin pontificō, from Latin pontifex (“high priest”), from pons (“bridge”) + facere (“make”).

parole.significato: Opium.
parole.testo: Calque of Medieval Latin lachryma papāveris (literally “tear of a poppy”).

parole.significato: To supply with inhabitants; to people.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin populātus, past participle of populor (“populate”), from Latin populus (“people”).

parole.significato: An honorific title given to a son of a reigning emperor in the Byzantine Empire, notably borne by Constantine VII Porph…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin porphyrogenitus, from Ancient Greek πορφυρογέννητος (porphurogénnētos, literally “born in the purple”).

parole.significato: Synonym of portreeve.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin portgravius, from Old English portgerēfa &c., from port + gerēfa (“reeve”).

parole.significato: A stroke added to a medieval punctus; a punctuation mark created by addition of such a stroke.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin positūra, feminine noun formed from positūrus (“about to place”). Doublet of posture.

parole.significato: After noon, in the afternoon.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Medieval Latin post merīdiem, from Latin post (“after”) + merīdiem, accusative singular of merīdiēs (“noon, midday”).

parole.significato: Relating to, or based on, practice or action rather than theory or hypothesis.
parole.testo: From Middle English practical, practicale, praktycall, from Medieval Latin practicālis.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to land or its products.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin praediālis, from Latin praedium (“farm, estate, land”).

parole.significato: An honorary canon of a cathedral or collegiate church.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin praebendārius, from Late Latin praebenda (“literally ‘things to be supplied’; prebend”), neuter plural of gerundive of praebeō (“supply”), from prae- (“pre-”) + habeō (“have, hold”).

parole.significato: A community of the Knights Templar, or the physical buildings or estate of such a community.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin praeceptoria, noun use of the feminine of praeceptorius (“commanding”), ultimately from praeceptor + -ius. Equivalent to preceptor + -y.

parole.significato: Precedence.
parole.testo: From Middle English precessioun, precession, from Medieval Latin prēcessiōn-, prēcessio, from Latin praecēdō.

parole.significato: An enclosed space having defined limits, normally marked by walls.
parole.testo: From Middle English precinct, precincte, early 15th century, in sense of “district for government purposes”, from Medieval Latin precinctum, alternative form of praecinctum (“enclosure, boundary line”), neuter singular of praecinctus, perfect passive participle of Latin praecingō (“surround, gird”),

parole.significato: A condition of favoring or liking; a tendency towards; proclivity; predisposition.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin praedīlēctiō.

parole.significato: An act or process that preempts; a preventive or forestalling action; as:
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin praeēmptiō (“previous purchase”), from praeemō (“buy before”), from Latin prae- (“before”) + emō (“buy”).

parole.significato: Relating to a preface.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin prefātia (“preface”) + English -al.

parole.significato: Serving as a preface or prelude; introductory, preliminary.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin *praefator + -ory (“agent”), from Medieval Latin prefatia (whence preface), for classical Latin praefatio (“a saying beforehand”) – see preface for details. Note that this is borrowed from Latin, not derived in English from preface, as in occasional misspelling *prefecatory.

parole.significato: A member of a Roman Catholic order of canons regular, founded by St Norbert c. 1120 in the town of Prémontré, France.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Praemonstrātēnsis (“pertaining to Prémontré”), from the Latin form of Prémontré, the town in Île-de-France where the order was founded.

parole.significato: To prepare.
parole.testo: From Middle English preparaten, from preparat + -en, from Medieval Latin preparātus, perfect passive participle of preparō. Equivalent to prepare + -ate (verb-forming suffix). In some recent uses, probably back-formation from preparation. Compare prepare, from Middle French.

parole.significato: prepared
parole.testo: From Middle English preparat, from Medieval Latin preparātus. See -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A provost: the presiding officer of various ecclesiastical bodies.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin prepositus, variant of praepositus (“[one] placed in charge”). Doublet of provost.

parole.significato: presbytership, eldership
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin presbyterātus. By surface analysis, presbyter + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, a body of people involved with it).

parole.significato: A presbyter or priest's wife.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin presbyterissa. By surface analysis, presbyter + -ess. Piecewise doublet of priestess.

parole.significato: The office or role of president.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin praesidentia. By surface analysis, president + -cy.

parole.significato: An instance of applying pressure; an instance of pressing.
parole.testo: From Middle English presse (“throng, crowd, clothespress”), partially from Old English press (“clothespress”) (from Medieval Latin pressa) and from Old French presse (Modern French presse) from Old French presser (“to press”), from Latin pressāre, from pressus, past participle of premere (“to press”

parole.significato: A claim or aspiration to a particular status or quality.
parole.testo: From Middle English pretencioun, pretensioun, from Medieval Latin prētēnsiō.

parole.significato: The act of preventing or hindering; obstruction of action, access, or approach; thwarting.
parole.testo: From Middle English prevencion, from Medieval Latin prēventiō.

parole.significato: Being the first in time or in history.
parole.testo: Probably partly from Medieval Latin prīmālis, from Latin prīmus (“first”) + -ālis, and partly from prime + -al.

parole.significato: A prayer or devotional book intended for laity, initially an abridgment of the breviary and manual including the hours…
parole.testo: From Middle English primer, primere, from Medieval Latin primarius and primarium (“prayer book”) possibly via Anglo-Norman primer (“prayer book”), from prima (“prime the liturgical hour and office”) + -arius and -arium (suffix forming related objects). Its use for schoolbooks derived from the late m

parole.significato: The outermost celestial sphere of the heavens in Ptolemaic astronomy, which was believed to cause all the inner spheres…
parole.testo: From Middle English primum mobile (“outermost celestial sphere causing other spheres to move”), borrowed from Medieval Latin prīmum mōbile (literally “first mover”), a calque of Arabic مُحَرِّك أَوَّل (muḥarrik ʔawwal, “first mover”), which is itself a calque of Ancient Greek τὸ πρῶτον κινῆσαν (tò p

parole.significato: The dignity, office, or government of a prior.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin priōrātus. By surface analysis, prior + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, the concrete charge of it). Compare French priorat.

parole.significato: A nun in charge of a priory (usually lower in rank than an abbess); mother superior.
parole.testo: From Middle English prieresse, priorasse, priores, prioresse, priorisse, priouresse, priures, priuresse, prowres, pryoras, pryorys, pryowresse, from Medieval Latin priōrissa and Old French prioresse, prieuresse; equivalent to prior + -ess.

parole.significato: The office of a procurator.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin prōcūrātorātus. By surface analysis, procurator + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a proem or proemium.
parole.testo: From Middle English prohemyal, from Medieval Latin proēmiālis.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to or characterized by prognosis or prediction.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin prognosticus, from Ancient Greek προγνωστικός (prognōstikós, “foreknowing”), from πρό (pró) + γνωστικός (gnōstikós, “of or for knowing, good at knowing”), from γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to learn to know, to perceive, to mark, to learn”).

parole.significato: To predict or forecast, especially through the application of skill.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin prognosticare; see prognostic for more.

parole.significato: Tending to prohibit, preclude, or disallow.
parole.testo: From Middle English prohibitif, prohibityve, from Medieval Latin prohibitīvus, from prohibit-, past-participle stem of Latin prohibēre. By surface analysis, prohibit + -ive.

parole.significato: An object intended to be or having been shot from a weapon.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin prōiectilis (“projectile”), from Latin prōiectus, perfect passive participle of prōiciō (“throw forth; extend; expel”).

parole.significato: A spokesman, one who speaks on behalf of others.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English prolocutor, a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin prōlocūtor.

parole.significato: Containing or consisting of a promise.
parole.testo: From Middle English promissorye, from Medieval Latin prōmissōrius. By surface analysis, promise + -ory.

parole.significato: A high point of land extending into a body of water, headland; cliff.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin prōmontōrium, from prōmineō, from prō- + *mineō (“to project or jut”, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to stand out”)) + -tōrium (“place”).

parole.significato: Serving to force the contents to move in a rapid outflow.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin propulsio (“term”), from Latin past participle of propello (“to drive forward, drive forth, drive away, drive out”).

parole.significato: The process of propelling, driving, or pushing, typically forward or onward; a propulsive force or impulse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin propulsio, propulsionis, from the past participle of Latin propello (“to drive forward, drive forth, drive away, drive out”).

parole.significato: A prosecuting attorney.
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1542, from Medieval Latin prosecutor, from prōsequor (English prosecute). By surface analysis, prosecute + -or.

parole.significato: A poetic composition consisting of both prose and verse, usually in alternation
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin prosimetrum.

parole.significato: Serving or intended to protect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōtēctīvus. By surface analysis, protect + -ive.

parole.significato: A chief legal clerk or notary in Roman Byzantium, and (hence) in Rome.
parole.testo: From Middle English prothonotarie, from Medieval Latin protonotarius, from Byzantine Greek πρωτονοτάριος (prōtonotários), from Ancient Greek πρῶτος (prôtos) + Byzantine Greek νοτάριος (notários), from Latin notārius (“notary”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to protocol.
parole.testo: From the Medieval Latin prōtocollārius.

parole.significato: Temporary; pending something more permanent.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin provisorius, from provis- (supine stem of provideo) + -orius (“-ory”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or produced by the lungs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pulmōnicus, from pulmō (“lung”).

parole.significato: Pulsating; that pulses.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pulsātilis, Latin pulsō + -ilis.

parole.significato: Prompt; on time.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūnctuālis (“relating to a point”), from Late Latin pūnctus (“point”) + -ālis (adjective suffix).

parole.significato: To add punctuation to.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūnctuātus, perfect passive participle of pūnctuō (“to mark with points”), from Medieval Latin pūnctus (“a point, dot”), from pungō (“to prick, punch”); see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of punch.

parole.significato: A set of symbols and marks which are used to clarify meaning in text by separating strings of words into clauses, phras…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin punctuātiō (“a marking with points, a writing, agreement”), from punctuō (“to mark with points, settle”). Morphologically, punctuate + -ion.

parole.significato: The basic dot (‧) used to end a sentence in medieval punctuation (ancestral to the full stop/period).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin punctus (“punctuation mark”).

parole.significato: A medieval punctuation mark indicating a short pause (approximately '̣).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pūnctus circumflexus (literally “bent-around mark”).

parole.significato: A medieval punctuation mark indicating a medium-length pause (approximately ⸵).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pūnctus ēlevātus (literally “raised mark”).

parole.significato: Synonym of punctus circumflexus.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pūnctus flexus (literally “bent mark”).

parole.significato: A medieval question mark, ⟨⹔⟩, possibly the ancestor of the modern mark ⟨?⟩.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pūnctus interrogātīvus (“question mark”).

parole.significato: A medieval punctuation mark marking the end of a sentence (approximately ;)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pūnctus versus (literally “facing mark”).

parole.significato: The period before puberty, or from birth to fourteen in males, and twelve in females
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūpillāritās.

parole.significato: The condition of being putrid; decay
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin putrēscentia.

parole.significato: Pyramid-shaped.
parole.testo: From Middle English piramidal, piramydale, from Medieval Latin pȳramidālis. By surface analysis, pyramid + -al.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an oracle or prophet, or to the telling of prophecies; oracular, prophetic.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English phitonic, phithonice (“of a possessing spirit: oracular, prophetic”), from Medieval Latin phitōnicus, a variant of Late Latin pȳthōnicus (“of or pertaining to divination, prophetic; magical”), from Byzantine Greek πυθωνικός (puthōnikós), from Koine Greek πύθων (púthōn, “spir

parole.significato: Scribal abbreviation of pre-.
parole.testo: An orthographic borrowing from Medieval Latin p͛-, an abbreviation of prae- (whence English pre-).

parole.significato: The higher division of the seven liberal arts in the Middle Ages, composed of geometry, astronomy, arithmetic, and musi…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin quadrivium (“the four mathematical studies”), from Latin quattuor (“four”) + via (“road”).

parole.significato: To assign a quantity to.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin quantifico (introduced by Sir William Hamilton in logic).

parole.significato: A period of 40 days, particularly
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin quarentena and quarentīna (“40-day period, Lent”) via Middle English quarentine, Norman quarenteine, French quarenteine, and Italian quarantina, via proposed Late Latin *quaranta + -ēna (forming distributive adjectives), from Latin quadrāgintā (“four tens, 40”). In reference to F

parole.significato: A site for mining stone, such as limestone, or slate.
parole.testo: From Middle English quarere, from Medieval Latin quarreria (1266), literally a “place where stones are squared”, from Old French quarrière (compare modern French carrière), from Vulgar Latin *quadraria, from Latin quadrō (“to square”), itself from quadra (“a square”), from quattuor (“four”), ultimat

parole.significato: One who has obsessive feelings of having been wronged.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin querulans, querulantis, ultimately from Latin querela.

parole.significato: A stillness or pause; something that quiets or represses; removal from activity.
parole.testo: Short for Medieval Latin quiētus est (literally “he is quiet”). First attested in the 1530s. Earlier attested as Late Middle English quietus est. Doublet of coy, quiet, quit, and quite.

parole.significato: Synonym of quinzieme, a tax of one fifteenth (6.7%).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin quindecima (“15th”), from quindecim (“15”). In reference to 2-week periods, based upon the Roman and medieval practice of counting inclusively.

parole.significato: The 14th day after a festival.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin quindena, from Latin quīndēnī (“15 each”), from the distributive form of quīndecim (“15”). It is used for a period of 14 days owing to the Roman and medieval practice of counting inclusively.

parole.significato: A moveable feast in the Christian calendar on the Sunday 49 days before Easter Sunday (50 days counting inclusively).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin quinquagesima dies (“50th day”).

parole.significato: Of or related to a set of 50 people or items.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin quinquagesimus (“fiftieth”) + -al.

parole.significato: A legal proceeding used to challenge the right of an individual or corporation to hold a public office or to exercise a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin quō warrantō (“by what warrant”).

parole.significato: A fragment of a human expression that is repeated by somebody else, for example from literature or a famous speech.
parole.testo: The obsolete sense of “quota”, from Medieval Latin quotātiō, from Latin quotāre, is attested from the 15th century. The sense “fragment of verbal expression”, attested from the 17th century, may come from this source, or else from the verb quote + -ation.

parole.significato: Arranged like rays that radiate from, or converge to, a common centre.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin radiālis (“radial”), from Latin radius. By surface analysis, radius + -al.

parole.significato: The process of taking root, or state of being rooted.
parole.testo: From Middle English radicacyon, from Medieval Latin rādīcātio.

parole.significato: A species of bellflower with roots and leaves formerly used in salads, Campanula rapunculus.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Medieval Latin rapuntium from Latin rapunculus, diminutive of rapum (“turnip”)

parole.significato: The wrinkling and creases on the inner surface of the wrist.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin rasceta, rasca, rascha, rasga, misread from Arabic رُسْغ (rusḡ).

parole.significato: The legal principle or rationale on which a judicial decision is based.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ratiō dēcidendī, from ratiō (“reckoning, method, reasoning”) + dēcidendī, genitive singular of dēcidendus, gerund of dēcidere (“to settle”).

parole.significato: A mineral, arsenic sulfide (AsS), often associated with orpiment and stibnite in lead, silver and gold ores.
parole.testo: From Middle English realgar, from Medieval Latin realgar, resalgar, from Arabic رَهْج اَلْغَار (rahj al-ḡār, literally “cave dust”).

parole.significato: To animate again.
parole.testo: From re- + animate (verb), probably after Medieval Latin reanimāre or French réanimer.

parole.significato: Capable of receiving something.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English receptive, receptyue (“capable of receiving something; acting as a receptacle”), borrowed from Medieval Latin receptivus (“capable of receiving something”), from Latin receptus (“retaken, having been retaken; received, having been received”) + -īvus (suffix added to the perf

parole.significato: A receptacle, a container .
parole.testo: From Middle English receptorie, from Medieval Latin receptorium (“a place of shelter”).

parole.significato: To recall; to collect one's thoughts again, especially about past events.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin recollectus (“remembered, composed”), from Latin recolligo (“gather again, recover”).

parole.significato: recoverable
parole.testo: From Middle English recuperable, from Medieval Latin recuperābilis and Old French recuperable. By surface analysis, recuperate + -able.

parole.significato: doubled
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin reduplicātus, from reduplicāre, from re- with duplicāre.

parole.significato: Referring back to the subject, or having an object equal to the subject.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin reflexīvus, from Latin reflexus, equivalent to reflex + -ive.

parole.significato: A household or commercial appliance used for keeping food fresh using refrigeration.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin refrīgerātor (“cooler”).

parole.significato: Royal rights, prerogatives and privileges actually enjoyed by any sovereign, regardless of his title (emperor, grand du…
parole.testo: From Middle English regalie, from Medieval Latin rēgālia (“royal powers”), substantivisation of the neuter plural of rēgālis (“of a king”), from rēx (“king”). By surface analysis, regal + -ia.

parole.significato: A system of government that substitutes for the reign of a king or queen when that king or queen becomes unable to rule.
parole.testo: From Middle English regencie (cf. regente), from Medieval Latin regentia, from Latin regēns, present participle of regō. By surface analysis, regent + -cy; compare also + -ency (“abstract-noun suffix”).

parole.significato: The killing of a king.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin rēgicidium (“king-killing”)

parole.significato: One who kills a king.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin rēgicida (“king-killer”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or resembling a queen.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin rēgīnālis, from rēgīna + -ālis.

parole.significato: To enter in a register; to enlist.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin registrum, from Late Latin regesta (“list, items recorded”), from Latin regerō (“to record, to carry back”), from re- + gerō (“to carry, bear”). Compare Latin registoria (“a treasurer”). Some senses influenced by association with unrelated Latin regō (“to rule”).

parole.significato: An official keeper or recorder of records.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin registrārius, from registrum (“register”) + -ārius (“agent of use”). See more at register. By surface analysis, register /registry (“a record”) + -ar.

parole.significato: A building in which things are registered or where registers are kept.
parole.testo: A variant of registery, from Middle English regestery (“?a record book; ?a bookmark”), partly from Medieval Latin regesterium, registerium and probably also partly formed with -ery. Equivalent to register + -y.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the reign of a monarch (or pope).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin rēgnālis, from Latin rēgnum + -ālis.

parole.significato: To restore (someone) to their former state, reputation, possessions, status etc.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin rehabilitātus, perfect passive participle of Latin rehabilitō. See habilitate.

parole.significato: Earnest protest or objection, disapproving pleading, or an act thereof.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Medieval Latin remōnstrātiō.

parole.significato: Relating to particular persons or things, each to each; particular; own.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin respectivus, from Latin respectus. By surface analysis, respect + -ive.

parole.significato: A legal doctrine which holds that an employer, officer, manager, supervisor, or other individual or group superior to a…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin respondeat superior (“let the superior respond or meet a charge”).

parole.significato: To proceed, spring up or rise, as a consequence, from facts, arguments, premises, combination of circumstances, consult…
parole.testo: Recorded since 1432 as Middle English resulten, from Medieval Latin resultare, in Classical Latin "to spring forward, rebound", the frequentative of the past participle of resilio (“to rebound”), from re- (“back”) + salio (“to jump, leap”).

parole.significato: A complex of blood vessels found in some vertebrates that preserves a gradient of a certain solute or particle, origina…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin rete mirabile (literally “wonderful net”) (14th century).

parole.significato: The thin layer of cells at the back of the eyeball that contains rods and cones sensitive to light, which trigger nerve…
parole.testo: From Middle English rethina, borrowing from Medieval Latin rētīna (“retina”, feminine noun), ellipsis of tunica rētīna (“net-like tunic”), used to describe the blood vessel system at the back of the eye. The phrase is attested in the 12th century in Guillelmus the abbot and Gerard of Cremona—the lat

parole.significato: Showing or characterized by reverence; respectful.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin reverentiālis, from Latin reverentia (“reverence”) + -ālis (adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: Any of the Ripuarian tribal section of the Frank people (comprising several tribes), who after some migration inhabited…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Ripuarius (perhaps from Latin ripa (“river bank”)) + -an.

parole.significato: A syrup made of evaporating fruit juice over a fire, usually mixed with sugar or honey, and especially used for medicin…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin rob, from Arabic ربّ (“thickened fruit juice”). Compare French rob, Spanish rob, Italian rob, robbo, Portuguese robe, arrobe, Persian ربودن (present stem: robâ).

parole.significato: Synonym of confirmation or ratification.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin rōborātiō (“strengthening, confirmation, validity”), from rōborāre (“to strengthen, to confirm”) + -tiō (“-tion: forming abstract nouns”), from rōbur (“reddish oak; hardness, strength”) + -āre (“forming verbs”). Equivalent to roborate + -tion.

parole.significato: Capable of rotation.
parole.testo: Attested mid 18th century, from Medieval Latin rotarius, from Latin rota (“wheel”).

parole.significato: A reddish aniline dye.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin rubīnus (“carbuncle, ruby”). Doublet of ruby.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Russia or Russians.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin (11th century) Russiānus, from Russia, a Latinization of the Old East Slavic Русь (Rusĭ)) + -ānus (“of or pertaining to”). Attested in English (both as a noun and as an adjective) from the 16th century. By surface analysis, Russia + -an. Piecewise doublet of Rossiyan.

parole.significato: A medieval armour covering for the foot, typically made of steel; a flexible armour shoe.
parole.testo: From Middle English sabatoun, from Medieval Latin sabatum, sabbatum. Compare sabatine and Old Provençal sabato.

parole.significato: A person who regards and keeps the seventh day of the week ("Saturday", the Israelite or Jewish Sabbath) as holy in con…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin sabbatarius, from Latin sabbatum, from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton), from Hebrew שבת (shabát) + -an. In use from c. 1610.

parole.significato: Relating to or denoting the suture on top of the skull which runs between the parietal bones in a front to back directi…
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Medieval Latin sagittālis, from sagitta (“an arrow, shaft, bolt”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: The code of laws of the Salian Franks, particularly the one excluding women from inheritance.
parole.testo: Calque of Medieval Latin Lex Salica.

parole.significato: Containing salt; salty.
parole.testo: PIE word  *sḗh₂l From Middle English salyne, from Medieval Latin salīna and Middle French salin, from Latin sal (“salt”).

parole.significato: The dorsal vein of the little finger, bleeding from which was anciently held to be a treatment for melancholy.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin salvatella, misread from salacella, misread from salaseilem, misread from alaseilem, from Arabic الْأُسَيْلِم (al-ʔusaylim).

parole.significato: sandalwood
parole.testo: From Middle English sandal (“sandalwood”), from Medieval Latin sandalum, from Byzantine Greek σάνδανον (sándanon), σάνταλον (sántalon), from Arabic صَنْدَل (ṣandal), from Middle Persian [script needed] (cndl /⁠čandal⁠/, “sandalwood”), from Sanskrit चन्दन (candana, “sandalwood”). Doublet of santalum.

parole.significato: Any of various tropical trees of the genus Santalum, native or long naturalized in India, Australia, Hawaii, and many s…
parole.testo: From sandal + wood, the first component being from Middle English sandal (“sandalwood”), from Medieval Latin sandalum, from Byzantine Greek σάνδανον (sándanon), σάνταλον (sántalon), from Arabic صَنْدَل (ṣandal), from Middle Persian [script needed] (cndl /⁠čandal⁠/, “sandalwood”), from Sanskrit चन्दन

parole.significato: Any of the genus Santalum of trees with entire opposite leaves and small apetalous flowers.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin sandalum, santalum. See sandal.

parole.significato: A prominent vein or nerve, the saphenous vein
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin saphena, from Arabic صَافِن (ṣāfin), from Hebrew צֹפֵן (ṣōfēn, “hiding”).

parole.significato: Having scabs.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin scabiōsus (“scabious”), from Latin scabiēs (see scabies); partly reinterpretable as scab + -ious.

parole.significato: Any of various herbaceous plants of the genus Scabiosa.
parole.testo: ] From Medieval Latin scabiōsa, substantivized from scabiōsus (“scabious”), see Etymology 1; the name comes from their medical use in the Middle Ages to cure scabies and leprosy.

parole.significato: An instrument, principally used in cupping, containing several lancets that are moved simultaneously by a spring, used…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin scarificātor.

parole.significato: An artful deviation from the ordinary arrangement of words.
parole.testo: From late Middle English scheame, from Medieval Latin schēma (“figure, form”), from Ancient Greek σχῆμα (skhêma, “form, shape”), from ἔχω (ékhō, “to hold”). Doublet of schema. Compare sketch.

parole.significato: A room set aside for the copying, writing, or illuminating of manuscripts and records, especially such a room in a mona…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin scrīptōrium, from Latin scrīptōrius (“pertaining to writing”). Doublet of escritoire.

parole.significato: Intense study of someone or something.
parole.testo: From Middle English scrutiny, from Medieval Latin scrūtinium (“a search, an inquiry”), from Vulgar Latin scrūtor (“to search or examine thoroughly”), from Late Latin scrūta (“rubbish, broken trash”), from an extension of Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”).

parole.significato: A tax, paid in lieu of military service, that was a significant source of revenue in England in the twelfth and thirtee…
parole.testo: From Middle English scutage, from Medieval Latin scutagium, from Latin scutum (“shield”).

parole.significato: A medium-sized deciduous tree of species Cordia myxa or, less often, Cordia latifolia, Cordia sebestena, or other speci…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin sebesten, from Arabic سِبِسْتَان (sibistān), from Persian سگپستان (sag-pestân, literally “dog teat”), from سگ (sag, “dog”) + پستان (pestân, “teat”).

parole.significato: The act of secluding, shutting out or keeping apart.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin, from Latin seclusio, from secludere.

parole.significato: A person who keeps records, takes notes and handles general clerical work.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin secrētārius (“one entrusted with secrets”), from Latin secrētus (“private, secret”), past participle of secernere (“to separate, set apart”), from se- (“apart”) + cernere (“to separate”).

parole.significato: The lay or temporal authority of a secular court to pronounce punishment (particularly capital punishment) of an offend…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English seculer arm, seculer arme (“civil authority or power”), a calque of Medieval Latin bracchium saeculāre (“(figurative) civil or lay power”), from Latin bracchium (“arm”) + saeculāre (neuter singular form of saeculāris (“profane, temporal, worldly”)).

parole.significato: The apparent radius of a star etc, when viewed from Earth.
parole.testo: From Middle English semidiametre, semydiametre, from Medieval Latin sēmidiameter, equivalent to semi- + diameter.

parole.significato: A measure of the amount of time a person has been a member of an organization, as compared to other members, and with a…
parole.testo: From Middle English senyoryte, from Medieval Latin senioritas, from Latin senior (“elder”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a seraph or the seraphim.

parole.significato: To verify something by supplying evidence; to authenticate or corroborate.

parole.significato: An abstract or a condensed presentation of the substance of a body of material.

parole.significato: Being everywhere at once: omnipresent.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being, or appearing to be, everywhere at once; actual or perceived omnipresence.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ubīquitās, from Latin ubīque.

parole.significato: Final; last in a series.

parole.significato: An instance or act of undulating.
parole.testo: From undulate + -ion, or borrowed from Medieval Latin undulātiō; compare French ondulation.

parole.significato: To pass urine from the body.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin urinātus, perfect passive participle of urinō (“urinate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), equivalent to urine + -ate. Compare French uriner.

parole.significato: The middle of the three concentric layers that make up the eye; it is pigmented and vascular, and comprises the choroid…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ūvea (“grape-like”), from Latin ūva (“grape”) + -ea, partial calque of Ancient Greek ῥαγοειδής χιτών (rhagoeidḗs khitṓn, “[covering] like a grape”), from ῥάξ (rháx, “grape”).

parole.significato: A pledge or security; bail.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin wadium, from Frankish *wadja, from Proto-Germanic *wadją (“pledge”); akin to Old English wedd (“pledge”). More at wed.

parole.significato: A living pledge, which exists where an estate is granted until a debt is paid out of its proceeds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin vadium vivum (“living pledge”).

parole.significato: To render valid.

parole.significato: Valid, validated.
parole.testo: First attested in 1586; borrowed from Medieval Latin validātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymolgy 1 for more.

parole.significato: Smallpox (Orthopoxvirus variola).

parole.significato: Capable of growth and reproduction, but not feeling or reason (often opposed to sensible and rational).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin vegetālis, from Latin vegetō.

parole.significato: The lowest degree of desire or volition; a total lack of effort to act.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin velleitās, from Latin velle (“wish, will”).

parole.significato: The pursuit of sexual indulgence or pleasure.
parole.testo: From Middle English venery, venerie, venerye, borrowed from Medieval Latin veneria, from venus (“love”).

parole.significato: Word for word; in exactly the same words as were used originally.
parole.testo: Attested in English since 1481 (therefore considered a Middle English derivation by some): from Medieval Latin verbātim (“word for word”), from Latin verbum (“word”) + -ātim (adverbial suffix).

parole.significato: Speaking truth; truthful; corresponding to facts.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin vērācitās, semantically equivalent to Latin vērāc- (etymological inchoation of vērāx) "true" > ver + -iloquent.

parole.significato: Vernix caseosa; a fatty deposit covering the skin of newborn babies.
parole.testo: Derived from Medieval Latin vernix (“varnish”).

parole.significato: vestry
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin vestiārium.

parole.significato: The hairs of plants, invertebrates and other non-mammalian organisms, taken as a whole.

parole.significato: able to be vindicated; justifiable
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin vindicābilis.

parole.significato: Eager to punish; vindicative.

parole.significato: Flight; flying.

parole.significato: To make clean by wiping; to wipe away.

parole.significato: Act of wiping clean; a cleansing; a purging.
parole.testo: From Middle English abstersioun, from either Old French or Medieval Latin abstertion, from Latin abstersus, past participle of abstergēo (“to wipe off or away”).

parole.significato: The act of abstracting, separating, withdrawing, or taking away; withdrawal; the state of being taken away.
parole.testo: From Middle English abstraccyone; either from Middle French abstraction or from Medieval Latin abstrāctiō (“separation”), from Latin abstrahō (“draw away”). Equivalent to abstract + -ion.

parole.significato: Belonging to the school or philosophy of Plato.

parole.significato: A dominion or region ruled by a duke or duchess.
